Let $n_e,n_b,n_c,n_g$ be nonnegative integers. For dimension zero, $\mathbb R^0$ has its single empty vector and its unique square matrix acts as the identity on that space. Choose real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, meaning $M_e^T=M_e$, $M_b^T=M_b$, $x^TM_ex>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and $y^TM_by>0$ for every nonzero $y\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$; these positivity conditions are vacuous on $\mathbb R^0$. Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. These are finite real matrix data; no mesh or continuum field is assumed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

For bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, in the metric sense of [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], its **Jordan outer content** is the infimum of $\sum_{r<q}\operatorname{vol}(R_r)$ over finite axis-parallel rectangle covers of $E$. Its **Jordan inner content** is the supremum of the same sums over finite families of rectangles contained in $E$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

Metric boundedness always supplies a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. For
nonempty $E$, choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^m$ and $r>0$ with
$E\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. Since
$|x_j-(x_0)_j|\le d_\infty(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,x_0)<r$ for every coordinate
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[def-metric-ball]]), the nondegenerate box
$\prod_{j<m}[(x_0)_j-r,(x_0)_j+r]$ contains $E$. The empty set lies in
any fixed nondegenerate rectangle.

Thus the outer family is nonempty and the same bounding rectangle bounds the
inner sums; the empty family gives inner sum $0$. Refining all listed
endpoints into one grid and splitting the nested finite sums shows every
inscribed sum is at most every covering sum
([[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Completeness therefore supplies finite real extrema
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]],
[[lem-sup-unique]]).

The set is **Jordan measurable** when the contents agree, and their common value is its **Jordan content**. The empty set and every degenerate rectangle have content $0$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

derivations.claim: Put $z=(e,b)\in\mathbb R^{n_e+n_b}$ and define $A:=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}S&M_e^{-1}C^TM_b\\-C&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $f(t):=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}j(t)\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The inverses exist by positive definiteness in [F1]: if $M_ex=0$, then $x^TM_ex=0$ forces $x=0$, and an injective square map in finite dimensions is invertible; the same holds for $M_b$. Thus the system is exactly $z'=Az+f(t)$.

Let $g(s):=e^{-(s-t_0)A}f(s)$ and $H(t):=\int_{t_0}^t g(s)\,ds$, interpreting each coordinate as a Riemann integral and using the oriented convention $\int_a^b=-\int_b^a$ when $b<a$ and $\int_a^a=0$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, then $g(s)$ and $H(t)$ are the unique empty vector for all $s,t$, so $H'=g$ vacuously. Otherwise, on every nondegenerate compact segment in $I$, each coordinate of $g$ is continuous, so [F3] gives integrability and [F4] defines $H$. For each coordinate $k$, the cut-additivity in [F6], together with the oriented convention, gives $H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)=\int_t^{t+h}g_k(s)\,ds$ whenever $t,t+h\in I$: positive-oriented additivity follows by splitting at an interior point, and reversing endpoints or using a zero-length interval gives the other endpoint orders. Thus, for $h\ne0$, $\frac{H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)}{h}-g_k(t)=\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds$, where [F7] evaluates the integral of the constant $g_k(t)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $g_k$ at $t$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|s-t|<\delta$; since $I$ is open, reduce $\delta$ so $[t-\delta,t+\delta]\subset I$. If $0<|h|<\delta$, then on $J=[\min(t,t+h),\max(t,t+h)]$ the absolute-value estimate and monotonicity in [F6], followed by [F7], give $\left|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds\right|\le\frac1{|h|}\int_J|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|\,ds\le\varepsilon$. Therefore each coordinate has derivative $g_k(t)$ and $H'(t)=g(t)$ throughout $I$.

Define $z(t):=e^{(t-t_0)A}(z_0+H(t))$, where $z_0=(e_0,b_0)$. By [F2] and step 1.2, the product rule gives $z'=Az+f(t)$, since $e^{(t-t_0)A}e^{-(t-t_0)A}=I$ by the commuting-product identity in [F2]; also $z(t_0)=z_0$. Thus a $C^1$ solution exists on all of $I$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, every state is the unique empty vector, so the solution is unique. Otherwise, if $\widetilde z$ is another solution with the same initial value, then $\xi(t):=e^{-(t-t_0)A}(\widetilde z(t)-z(t))$ has derivative zero by [F2] and the two differential equations. Each coordinate of $\xi$ is constant by [F5] and vanishes at $t_0$, so $\widetilde z=z$.

Differentiate $W=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$ and substitute the system equations. Symmetry of $M_e,M_b$ gives $\dot W=e^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)+b^TM_b(-Ce)=-e^TSe-e^Tj$, because the real scalar cross terms $e^TC^TM_bb$ and $b^TM_bCe$ are equal and cancel.
The magnetic quantity satisfies $(Db)'=D\dot b=-DCe=0$ by [F1]; each coordinate is constant by [F5], and its value at $t_0$ is $Db(t_0)$.
Since $q=-G^TM_ee$, differentiation and the first system equation give $\dot q=-G^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)=-(CG)^TM_bb+G^T(Se+j)=G^T(Se+j)$, using $CG=0$ from [F1]. This proves all three identities.

derivations.claim: Put $C:=m^2-q^2$ and $w:=\psi^2$. Since $2r+m>0$, the condition $w>0$ is equivalent to $2r+m>|q|$, giving exactly $\mathcal D_{m,q}$. Thus $\psi$ is smooth and positive there. In Euclidean spherical coordinates, $\bar D_i\bar E^i=r^{-2}\partial_r(r^2 q r^{-2})=0$, while $\bar D_i\bar B^i=0$.

On this domain $w:=\psi^2=1+m/r+C/(4r^2)$, $w'=-m/r^2-C/(2r^3)$, and $w''=2m/r^3+3C/(2r^4)$. Since $\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}\psi=\psi''+2\psi'/r$, $\psi'/\psi=w'/(2w)$ and $\psi''/\psi=w''/(2w)-(w')^2/(4w^2)$ give $\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}\psi/\psi=(w''/2+w'/r)/w-(w')^2/(4w^2)=(Cw/r^4-(w')^2)/(4w^2)=-q^2/(4r^4w^2)$; here $w''/2+w'/r=C/(4r^4)$ and direct expansion gives $Cw/r^4-(w')^2=-q^2/r^4$. Thus $\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}\psi=-q^2/(4r^4\psi^3)$. With $\bar R=0$, $\bar A=\tau=\Lambda=\bar B=0$, the transformed scalar equation is $-8\Delta\psi-2q^2r^{-4}\psi^{-3}=0$.

The seed Gauss constraint holds by step 1.1, and step 1.2 verifies the Hamiltonian equation. The momentum right side vanishes because $\bar B=0$, and its left side vanishes because $K=\tau=0$. The omitted point $r=0$ is not in the manifold, so the smooth divergence calculation on $\mathcal D_{m,q}\times S^2$ makes no distributional assertion at the puncture.

Suppose $m>|q|$, so $C>0$ and $r_0=\sqrt C/2$. Then $R_{\rm areal}=r+m+C/(4r)$, $R'_{\rm areal}=1-C/(4r^2)$, and $R''_{\rm areal}=C/(2r^3)>0$. Hence $R_{\rm areal}$ has its unique minimum on $(0,\infty)$ at $r_0$, with value $m+\sqrt C$. The area formula follows directly from the induced metric on $S_r$, namely $r^2\psi^4\gamma_{S^2}$.

The outward unit normal to $S_r$ is $\nu=\psi^{-2}\partial_r$. Its mean curvature, defined as the trace of the second fundamental form, is $H=\operatorname{div}_h\nu=(\sqrt{\det h})^{-1}\partial_r(\sqrt{\det h}\,\psi^{-2})=2R'_{\rm areal}/(\psi^2R_{\rm areal})$. Thus $H(r_0)=0$, and $H$ is nonzero for every other centered coordinate sphere.

Write $r_0^2=C/4$ and $R=R_{\rm areal}(r)$. On $r>r_0$, $R>m+2r_0$, so $f(R)>0$. Direct algebra gives $R^2f(R)=(R-m)^2-C=(r-r_0^2/r)^2$ and $dR/dr=1-r_0^2/r^2=(r-r_0^2/r)/r$. Therefore $f(R)^{-1}(dR/dr)^2=R^2/r^2=\psi^4$, which proves that $h=\psi^4dr^2+R^2\gamma_{S^2}$ equals the radial and angular spatial metric in [F3] on this branch.

As $r\to\infty$, $\psi^4=1+2m/r+O(r^{-2})$; differentiating this explicit rational expression for $\psi^4$ gives first- and second-coordinate-derivative falloffs $O(r^{-2})$ and $O(r^{-3})$. For the inner end put $\tilde r=r_0^2/r$. Then $\psi(r)^2r^2/r_0^2=1+m/\tilde r+r_0^2/\tilde r^2=\psi(\tilde r)^2$ and $dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2}=(r^4/r_0^4)(d\tilde r^2+\tilde r^2\gamma_{S^2})$. Hence the inner metric is exactly the same isotropic form in $\tilde r$, and it has the same falloff and derivative estimates. This proves the two stated end descriptions without extending the static areal chart through $f=0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

citations.quote: Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

Assume Countable Choice, meaning that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable oriented four-manifold without boundary. A continuous real top form is a continuous section of $\Lambda^4T^*M$: in every smooth coordinate chart it has the form $f(x)\,dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4$ with continuous real coefficient $f$, and the coefficients transform by the determinant of the coordinate-transition derivative. Its support is the closure in $M$ of its nonzero locus. Write $C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$ for these forms with compact support.

For $\omega\in C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$, put $K=\operatorname{supp}\omega$. If $K=\varnothing$, define its integral to be zero. Otherwise choose finitely many positively oriented charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$ and smooth functions $\chi_i:M\to[0,1]$ with compact support contained in $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Write
$$
(\phi_i^{-1})^*(\chi_i\omega)=f_i\,dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4
$$
on $\phi_i(U_i)$ and extend $f_i$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$, obtaining $\widetilde f_i$. Define
$$
\mathcal I_M(\omega):=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^4}\widetilde f_i(x)\,dx,
$$
where each Euclidean integral is the Riemann integral over any closed nondegenerate rectangle whose interior contains its support. Such finite cutoffs exist, each zero extension is continuous and compactly supported, and the value is independent of the chosen charts, cutoffs and bounding rectangles. This is a linear functional on $C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$. For fixed cutoffs and bounding rectangles $Q_i$, it satisfies $|\mathcal I_M(\omega)|\le\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)\sup_{Q_i}|\widetilde f_i|$; thus uniform convergence of these finitely many zero-extended coefficients implies convergence of their integrals. If an open set $V\subseteq M$ contains $K$, then $\mathcal I_V(\omega|_V)=\mathcal I_M(\omega)$, with the restricted orientation. On smooth compactly supported top forms it equals the previously defined smooth manifold integral.

Countable Choice is retained to match that smooth integral's standing convention. The finite-cover construction and comparison for continuous coefficients below require no further choice principle, and do not assume the full Axiom of Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The compact-support integral on an oriented manifold is independent of the chart cover, coordinate maps, subordinate partition, and refinement. If $U\subset M$ is open and contains $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, with its restricted orientation, then $\int_U\omega|_U=\int_M\omega$.

derivations.claim: Each contraction defining $X$ and $Y$ is a scalar under changes of coordinates, because $g^{-1}$ and $\star_g$ are tensorial. Since $F$, $g$, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$ are smooth, $X,Y$ are smooth; $L_X(X,Y)$ and $L_Y(X,Y)$ are $C^1$. Therefore $H$ is a globally defined $C^1$ section of $\Lambda^2TM$, and the displayed action density is a globally defined $C^1$ top form.

For a permitted compactly supported variation $a$, [F3] gives $F_\epsilon-F=\epsilon da$, which vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}a$. Hence the difference of the two $L$ densities is compactly supported. Its coefficient is at least continuous, so the integral $\mathcal I_M$ in [F4] is finite without requiring a smooth density. On finitely many fixed chart rectangles near that support, the chain rule gives continuous parameter derivatives; their uniform convergence of difference quotients on compact rectangles allows passage to the integrals by the rectangle bound in [F4]. Hence its first variation is well-defined for $L\in C^2$, with no stronger regularity assumption. Thus the Definition specifies a relative action and stationarity predicate without assuming the unvaried action is finite or that a stationary connection exists.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, independent orientation $o$, and the torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla$ selected by $g$. Fix a smooth principal $U(1)$ bundle sector and a smooth connection $\mathcal A$ in that sector. In the inherited physical-curvature normalization, its curvature is a smooth real two-form $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $dF=0$. A permitted variation is $\mathcal A_\epsilon=\mathcal A+\epsilon a$, where $a\in\Omega^1(M)$ is smooth and compactly supported; the same-sector convention gives $F_\epsilon=F+\epsilon da$. No global potential is required.

Raise indices with $g^{-1}$ and let $\star_g$ be the Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$. Define the scalar invariants
$X:=-\frac14 F_{ab}F^{ab},\qquad Y:=-\frac14F_{ab}(\star_gF)^{ab}.$
Let $L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and write $L_X,L_Y$ for its first partial derivatives evaluated at $(X,Y)$. Define the contravariant antisymmetric tensor
$H^{ab}:=L_XF^{ab}+L_Y(\star_gF)^{ab}.$
The source-free local action density is $L(X,Y)\,\mathrm{vol}_g$. Its relative action difference under a compact variation is the integral of $[L(X(F_\epsilon),Y(F_\epsilon))-L(X(F),Y(F))]\,\mathrm{vol}_g$; this difference has compact support even when the unvaried integral over $M$ is not finite. The connection is stationary when the derivative of this relative action at $\epsilon=0$ vanishes for every permitted $a$.

In the mathematical normalization, $L=X$ is the Maxwell quadratic term. If units are attached, the components of $F$ have a fixed unit $\mathfrak F$, $X,Y,L$ have unit $\mathfrak F^2$, and coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ in $L=X+\alpha X^2+\beta Y^2$ have unit $\mathfrak F^{-2}$, so $\alpha X$ and $\beta Y$ are dimensionless. This normalization is not an SI action prefactor. The coefficients are arbitrary parameters, not QED coefficients. This definition supplies no quantum origin, source coupling, characteristic-cone condition, hyperbolicity, causality, or solution-existence claim.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

[A1] The smooth tangent-bundle structure used by the existing Lorentzian and observer definitions is recorded under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Its exact statement is that each countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. No full Axiom of Choice is used by the finite local construction below. ([[def-countable-choice]])

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with the metric
volume form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ and metric-selected connection $\nabla$. Let
$F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and let $c,\mu_0>0$ be fixed
real coefficients. The action density is

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{EM}}\,\mathrm{vol}_g=-\frac{1}{4\mu_0c}F_{ab}F^{ab}\,\mathrm{vol}_g=-\frac{1}{2\mu_0c}F\wedge\star_gF.$$

When this density has a global integral, denote it by $S_{\mathrm{EM}}[g,F]$.
On a noncompact domain, every displayed variation below means the finite
action difference supported by the compactly supported variation.

Assume the fixed smooth bundle sector and connection-variation interface in
[A1] below. Then:

**(a) Connection variation.** For every smooth compactly supported global
one-form $\alpha$ allowed by that fixed-sector interface, holding $g$ fixed gives $\delta F=d\alpha$ and

$$\delta_A S_{\mathrm{EM}}[\alpha]=\frac{1}{\mu_0c}\int_M(\nabla_aF^{ab})\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

If a differentiable source-sector functional on the same variations satisfies
$\delta_A S_{\mathrm{m}}[\alpha]=c^{-1}\int_Mj^b\alpha_b\,\mathrm{vol}_g$ for a
smooth vector field $j$, then stationarity of
$S_{\mathrm{EM}}+S_{\mathrm m}$ under every such $\alpha$ is equivalent on $M$ to

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b,$$

and hence to $d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$ by
[[lem-emg-maxwell-current-forms]]. This is a conditional variational
calculation; it asserts no matter-action existence or physical adoption.

**(b) Metric variation.** For a smooth compactly supported symmetric inverse
metric variation $q^{ab}:=\delta g^{ab}$, holding the lower components
$F_{ab}$ fixed and preserving Lorentz signature for sufficiently small
parameter, define $T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}$ by

$$\delta_gS_{\mathrm{EM}}[q]=-\frac{1}{2c}\int_M T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}q^{ab}\,\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Then

$$T_{\mathrm{EM},ab}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right).$$

This is the tensor obtained by varying the free electromagnetic action; it
contains no stress contribution from a source or matter functional.

[A1] The current batch-2 carriers [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]] and [[lem-emg-circle-connection-gluing]] exist, and their inspected interface matches the use here: $F=\kappa_0 f$ is the physical curvature two-form of a normalized connection on a fixed principal $U(1)$ bundle, given by a supplied countable open cover, smooth transition cocycle and compatible local forms; the gluing lemma states that two connections with the same transitions differ by a global smooth base one-form, so a compactly supported global physical one-form $\alpha$ is an allowed variation and $\delta F=d\alpha$. The normalization $\kappa_0>0$ rescales the circle connection and is not identified with $\hbar$ or an electric charge. Both carriers are currently draft; the gluing construction now uses the actual set-size definition authored on emg-mg02, together with the other six typed foundational conventions on that page. The fixed-sector variation interface is unchanged. These authored drafts do not assert independent acceptance.

[F5] The geometric suppliers inherit $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, whose exact statement is that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]). The local variational calculation uses no additional choice.

[F12] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a smooth chart cover admits a smooth subordinate partition of unity ([[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]]). The integral of a compactly supported top form is its finite sum of chart integrals ([[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]]), independent of cover and partition ([[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]]). In a positive chart the metric volume coefficient is $w$.
