Assume Countable Choice for the smooth Lorentzian tangent-bundle conventions of the suppliers. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, $r_0>0$, and $\mathcal E=I\times(r_0,\infty)\times S^2$, where $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ has its unit round metric $q_{AB}$ and area form $d\Omega$. Let $D_A$ be the Levi-Civita covariant derivative of $q$, and raise angular indices with $q^{AB}$. A **Bondi-Sachs end** is a smooth Lorentzian metric on $\mathcal E$ written in coordinates $(u,r,x^A)$, $A,B=1,2$, as

$$g=-\left(e^{2\beta}\frac Vr-r^2\gamma_{AB}U^AU^B\right)du^2-2e^{2\beta}du\,dr-2r^2\gamma_{AB}U^Bdu\,dx^A+r^2\gamma_{AB}dx^A dx^B,$$

where $\beta,V,U^A,\gamma_{AB}$ are smooth, $\gamma_{AB}$ is positive definite, $\gamma^{AC}\gamma_{CB}=\delta^A_B$, and $\det(\gamma_{AB})=\det(q_{AB})$. Thus $u=\mathrm{constant}$ are outgoing null hypersurfaces, $r$ is the area radius, and $x^A$ are constant along their null generators. This Bondi gauge has $g_{rr}=g_{rA}=0$.

A **smooth Bondi expansion** is such an end with the differentiated uniform expansions

$$\gamma_{AB}=q_{AB}+\frac{C_{AB}(u,x)}r+\frac{P_{AB}(u,x)}{r^2}+O(r^{-3}),\qquad \beta=O(r^{-2}),\qquad U^A=\frac{U^A_{(2)}(u,x)}{r^2}+\frac{U^A_{(3)}(u,x)}{r^3}+O(r^{-4}),\qquad V=r-2m(u,x)+\frac{V_{(1)}(u,x)}r+O(r^{-2}).$$

Here $C_{AB}$, $P_{AB}$ and the displayed coefficients are smooth sphere fields on $I$; the determinant gauge imposes $q^{AB}C_{AB}=0$ and $q^{AB}P_{AB}=\tfrac12 C_{AB}C^{AB}$. For every compact $I'\subset I$, angular chart compact set, and derivative multi-index $\alpha$ of total order at most two, the partial derivatives of each $O(r^{-k})$ remainder obey $\partial_u^{\alpha_u}D^{\alpha_x}\partial_r^{\alpha_r}O(r^{-k})=O(r^{-k-\alpha_r})$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$. Define the **mass aspect** $m$ by the $r^{-1}$ coefficient in $V$, the **Bondi shear** by $C_{AB}=\lim_{r\to\infty}r(\gamma_{AB}-q_{AB})$, the **Bondi news** by $N_{AB}:=\partial_u C_{AB}$, and the **geometric Bondi mass** by $m_B(u):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}m(u,x)\,d\Omega$. The future null boundary used here is the formal $r\to\infty$ boundary $\mathcal I^+=I\times S^2$ with coordinates $(u,x^A)$; no conformal completion is included in this definition. A **vacuum Bondi expansion** means, in addition, that the Ricci tensor $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ defined by the curvature convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] vanishes to the asymptotic coefficient orders under discussion, with no cosmological term.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart $x$ and metric components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Since the chart identifies each
$T_p\mathbb R^4$ with $\mathbb R^4$, all objects below are defined by their
components in this chart; they are the components at a point, and a subscript
$p$ is suppressed. Indices are raised and lowered with $\eta$ and $\eta^{-1}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]), and orthogonality is in
the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]].

**(a) Observer, propagation direction, screen.** Let $n=n^a\partial_a$ be an
**observer** of the flat model: $n$ is future-directed, $\eta(n,n)=-1$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); and let
$s=s^a\partial_a$ be a **propagation direction**: $\eta(s,s)=1$ and
$\eta(n,s)=0$. The pair defines the two-dimensional **screen**
$\Sigma(n,s):=\{v\in\mathbb R^4:\eta(v,n)=0,\ \eta(v,s)=0\}$, on which the
restriction of $\eta$ is positive definite by
[[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]. The **screen projector** and
the **spatial projector** of the pair are the $(1,1)$-tensors with components

$$p^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b-s^as_b,\qquad h^a{}_b:=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b,$$

and the covariant form of the screen projector is
$p_{ab}:=\eta_{ac}p^c{}_b=\eta_{ab}+n_an_b-s_as_b$. The properties $p^2=p$,
$h^2=h$, $\operatorname{im}p=\Sigma(n,s)$ and $\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$
are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page.

**(b) TT projection.** Let $A=(A_{ab})$ be a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
at a point. Its **transverse-traceless (TT) projection with respect to
$(n,s)$** is the symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$\Pi_{n,s}(A)_{ab}:=p_a{}^cp_b{}^dA_{cd}-\tfrac12\,p_{ab}\,p^{cd}A_{cd},\qquad p^{cd}:=\eta^{ce}\eta^{df}p_{ef}.$$

**(c) Screen amplitudes.** Let $(e_1,e_2)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $\Sigma(n,s)$ (which exists by
[[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]] applied
to the positive-definite restriction of $\eta$). For a symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor $A$ the **plus and cross amplitudes of $A$ with respect to
$(e_1,e_2)$** are $A_+:=A(e_1,e_1)$ and $A_\times:=A(e_1,e_2)$; if $A$ is
TT with respect to $(n,s)$ in the sense of clause (d) below, then, extending
the screen dual basis to covectors on $\mathbb R^4$ by
$e^i(v):=\eta(e_i,v)$ for $i=1,2$ (so both vanish on $n,s$),

$$A=A_+\bigl(e^1\otimes e^1-e^2\otimes e^2\bigr)+A_\times\bigl(e^1\otimes e^2+e^2\otimes e^1\bigr).$$

For a TT screen tensor $A$, under the rotation
$e_1'=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$,
$e_2'=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$ of the screen basis the amplitudes
transform as $A_+'=A_+\cos2\theta+A_\times\sin2\theta$ and
$A_\times'=-A_+\sin2\theta+A_\times\cos2\theta$. Here $\sin$ and $\cos$
are the power-series functions of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]];
expanding $A(e_1',e_1')$ and $A(e_1',e_2')$ by bilinearity and applying the
addition formulas of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] gives the two
displayed transformations.

**(d) TT tensors and TT perturbations.** A symmetric covariant $2$-tensor
$A$ is **transverse-traceless (TT) with respect to $(n,s)$** when
$A(n,\cdot)=0$, $A(s,\cdot)=0$ and $\eta^{ab}A_{ab}=0$. For a symmetric
field $h$ on a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, use the
constant smooth extensions of the fixed component vectors:
$n_q:=n^a\partial_a|_q$ and $s_q:=s^a\partial_a|_q$ for $q\in\Omega$.
Here a symmetric field is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field with symmetric
components in the sense of [[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]]. Then
"TT with respect to $(n,s)$" means
$h_q(n_q,\cdot)=h_q(s_q,\cdot)=0$ and $\eta^{ab}h_{ab}(q)=0$ for every
$q\in\Omega$. It is **spatial with respect to $n$** when
$h_q(n_q,\cdot)=0$ for every $q\in\Omega$.

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the screen, the two projections and the
amplitude terminology, and states the rotation law of clause (c) as part of
the naming. It asserts no property of $\Pi_{n,s}$ (idempotence, rank, image
and trace are proved in the screen-projector lemma of this page), no relation
to the planar perturbations of the plane-wave definition of this page
(established in the gauge-decomposition lemma of this page) and no physical
interpretation of the amplitudes.

Let $(M,g,N)=(\mathbb R^4,\eta,\partial_0)$ be the flat model with its
inertial chart and let $(\varepsilon_1,h,q)$ be a flat linearized family over
an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with first-order coefficients
$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}$ as in [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]]; write
$R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)$ for the curvature components of $g(\lambda)$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]) and define the
**first-order curvature coefficient**

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}:=\partial_\lambda R^a{}_{bcd}(\lambda)\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}:=\eta_{ae}R^{(1)e}{}_{bcd}.$$

Then:

**(a) General first-order formula.** The coefficient is defined (the
component family is differentiable in $\lambda$ at $0$) and

$$R^{(1)a}{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{cb},\qquad R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_b\partial_ch_{ad}+\partial_a\partial_dh_{bc}-\partial_a\partial_ch_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dh_{ac}\bigr).$$

**(b) Gauge invariance.** For every smooth covector field $\xi$ on $\Omega$,
with $h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a$ the gauge-transformed
perturbation of [[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (d),
$R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h')=R^{(1)}_{abcd}(h)$: the first-order curvature coefficient
is unchanged by gauge transformations.

**(c) Planar and TT waves.** Let $F=(F_{ab})$ be a smooth planar profile with
$h_{ab}(x)=F_{ab}(u(x))$, $u=x^0-x^3$, and let $n_a=\partial_au$; then

$$R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\tfrac12\bigl(n_bn_cF''_{ad}+n_an_dF''_{bc}-n_an_cF''_{bd}-n_bn_dF''_{ac}\bigr).$$

If the profile is spatial ($F_{0a}=0$ for all $a$), then
$R^{(1)}_{0i0j}=-\tfrac12F''_{ij}$ and, raising indices,
$R^{(1)i}{}_{00j}=+\tfrac12F''{}^i{}_j$. If the profile is TT with amplitudes
$A_+,A_\times$, then $F''$ is supported on the screen with $F''_{11}=A_+''$,
$F''_{22}=-A_+''$, $F''_{12}=F''_{21}=A_\times''$ and all other second
derivatives of the profile zero; in particular

$$R^{(1)}_{0101}=-\tfrac12A_+'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0102}=-\tfrac12A_\times'',\qquad R^{(1)}_{0202}=+\tfrac12A_+'' .$$

**(d) Contraction to the Ricci coefficient.** For every perturbation $h$,

$$\eta^{ac}R^{(1)}_{abcd}=\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd},$$

the right-hand side being the first-order coefficient of
[[def-gr-flat-linearized-perturbation]] clause (b). For a TT planar
perturbation both sides vanish: $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{bd}=0$ and
$S^{(1)}=0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $R$ be its
curvature ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let
$I,J_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be intervals with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]), and let $F:J_0\times I\to M$ be a smooth map. Write
$T:=\partial_tF$ and $J^F:=\partial_rF$; a field along $F$ means a smooth
section of $F^*TM$ over $J_0\times I$, and $D_r,D_t$ are the covariant
derivatives in the two parameters
([[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Curvature as the commutator of the two derivatives.** For every smooth
field $V$ along $F$,
$$\bigl(D_tD_r-D_rD_t\bigr)V=R(T,J^F)V .$$

**(b) Geodesic deviation.** Suppose in addition that for every $r\in J_0$ the
curve $t\mapsto F(r,t)$ is a geodesic with affine parameter $t$, that is
$D_tT=0$. Then $D_tJ^F=D_rT$ and
$$D_t^2J^F=R(T,J^F)T .$$
Consequently, for every $r$ the field $t\mapsto J^F(r,t)$ is a Jacobi field
along the geodesic $t\mapsto F(r,t)$
([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (b)), and for a geodesic
variation the variation field is a Jacobi field.

**(c) Initial data.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth geodesic and let
$s_0\in I$. For every pair $J_0,J_1\in T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$ there exists exactly
one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(s_0)=J_0,\qquad D_sJ(s_0)=J_1 .$$
The set of all Jacobi fields along $\gamma$ is a real vector space of
dimension $8$, and $J\mapsto\bigl(J(s_0),D_sJ(s_0)\bigr)$ is a linear
isomorphism onto $T_{\gamma(s_0)}M\oplus T_{\gamma(s_0)}M$.

**(d) The tangential component.** Let $\gamma$ be a smooth geodesic and $J$ a
smooth Jacobi field along it. Then $s\mapsto g(J,\gamma')(s)$ is affine, and
if $\gamma$ is future timelike with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-1$, the normal
component $J^\perp$ of [[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause
(e), explicitly $J^\perp=J+g(J,\gamma')\gamma'$, is again a Jacobi field
along $\gamma$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the flat model of
[[def-gr-minkowski-model-and-inertial-chart]] with inertial chart $x$ and
constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, identified with its image under
$x$; all components below are taken in the inertial chart. Let $c>0$ be a
real parameter.

**(a) Flat linearized family.** A **flat linearized family over $\Omega$**
consists of a number $\varepsilon_1>0$, a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field $h$ on $\Omega$ with components $h_{ab}$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]) — the **first-order
perturbation** — and a smooth family $q$ of symmetric component fields
$q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$, defined for $\lambda\in(-\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_1)$
and $p\in\Omega$, such that for every $\lambda$ with
$0<|\lambda|<\varepsilon_1$ the component field

$$g_{ab}(\lambda,p):=\eta_{ab}+\lambda\,h_{ab}(p)+\lambda^2\,q_{ab}(\lambda,p)$$

is the component field of a smooth Lorentzian metric $g(\lambda)$ on
$\Omega$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $q$ is the **normalized remainder**. The
family is thus normalized so that $g(0)=\eta$ is its value at
$\lambda=0$ and $h=\partial_\lambda g(\lambda)|_{\lambda=0}$. No assumption
is made that $g(\lambda)$ solves any field equation; the metrics $g(\lambda)$
are the mathematical input of the linearization.

**(b) First-order coefficients.** Let $A(\lambda)$ stand for any of the
component families $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))$, $S(g(\lambda))$,
$G_{ab}(g(\lambda))$ of the metric-selected connection of $g(\lambda)$; these
are smooth in $(\lambda,p)$ because the Christoffel symbols, the curvature
components and the inverse metric are smooth functions of the metric
components and their derivatives
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Define the **first-order
coefficients**

$$\Gamma^{(1)a}{}_{bc}:=\partial_\lambda\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\quad \operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},$$
$$S^{(1)}:=\partial_\lambda S(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0},\qquad G^{(1)}_{ab}:=\partial_\lambda G_{ab}(g(\lambda))\big|_{\lambda=0}.$$

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices on first-order quantities are raised and
lowered with the flat metric $\eta$ and its inverse $\eta^{ab}$
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]): $\partial^a:=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$,
$h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$, and

$$\Box:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b=-\partial_0^2+\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2$$

is the **d'Alembertian** of the flat metric, applied componentwise to
component families. The **trace** of $h$ and the **trace-reversed
perturbation** are

$$h:=\eta^{ab}h_{ab},\qquad \bar h_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,h\,\eta_{ab} .$$

The inverse passage is the same formula, $\bar h_{ab}$'s trace being
$\eta^{ab}\bar h_{ab}=h-2h=-h$: explicitly

$$h_{ab}=\bar h_{ab}-\tfrac12\,\eta_{ab}\,\eta^{cd}\bar h_{cd} .$$

**(d) Gauge transformation.** For a smooth covector field $\xi_b$ on
$\Omega$ define the **gauge-transformed first-order perturbation**

$$h'_{ab}:=h_{ab}-\partial_a\xi_b-\partial_b\xi_a .$$

This is the first-order perturbation of the pullback family
$\Phi_{-\lambda}^*g(\lambda)$ along the local flows $\Phi_s$ of the vector
field $\xi^a=\eta^{ab}\xi_b$, that is, the perturbation produced by the
infinitesimal chart change $x'^a=x^a+\lambda\xi^a$ and re-read on the fixed
inertial chart; the transformation of the metric components displayed here
is the linearization of the Jacobian transformation law, and
its consequences for $\bar h$ and for $\operatorname{Ric}^{(1)}$, $S^{(1)}$
and $G^{(1)}$ are proved separately on this page (the first-order curvature
and gauge theorem that follows this definition).
The perturbation $h$ is **in harmonic gauge** (also called de Donder gauge)
when

$$\partial^a\bar h_{ab}=0 .$$

**(e) Scope.** This item fixes the objects of the flat linearization: the
normalized family, the first-order coefficients defined as exact
$\lambda$-derivatives, the trace reversal, the d'Alembertian and the gauge
transformation. It asserts no explicit formula for the first-order
coefficients, no existence of a gauge representative satisfying (d), no
solution of any linearized field equation and no physical interpretation;
those are separate results. The notation is tied to the inertial chart: a
change of chart is a different operation from the gauge transformation (d),
which changes the metric family inside the fixed chart.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Apply [F5] to each smooth tensor component $C_{AB}(u,x)$ at the fixed angular point. Since $N_{AB}=\partial_uC_{AB}$, $C_{AB}(u_2,x)-C_{AB}(u_1,x)=\int_{u_1}^{u_2}N_{AB}(u,x)\,du$. This is the first identity.

In the adapted frame of [A2], the plane-wave curvature supplier gives $R^{(1)A}{}_{00B}=\tfrac12\partial_u^2H^A{}_B$ ([F3]); the Jacobi equation of [F4] with initial screen value $s_0^Ae_A$ and zero initial derivative therefore has this forcing at first order, since the flat background curvature is zero and the basis is constant. Thus its formal first-order response obeys exactly the defining equation for $\delta s^A$ in the Statement. No finite-amplitude error estimate is used.

For the quantitative clause set $T:=u_2-u_1>0$. Choose a compact state neighborhood of $(\gamma_0(u),\partial_0)$, $u\in[u_1,u_2]$, whose position projection lies inside the specified open tube, with positive margins about this compact graph. By [F6] and [F8], the Christoffels are smooth jointly and vanish at $\lambda=0$, so their norms on this neighborhood are at most $C|\lambda|$ for small $|\lambda|$. The coordinate geodesic system is $x'=v$, $v'^a=-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\lambda,x)v^bv^c$. By [F7] it has a local smooth solution from the stated unit initial velocity. As long as it stays in this neighborhood, the bounded velocity range gives $|v-\partial_0|\le|v(u_1)-\partial_0|+C_1|\lambda|T$ and $|x-\gamma_0|\le T\sup|v-\partial_0|$. Choose $|\lambda|$ small enough to keep both bounds strictly inside the chosen margins. The solution cannot leave the neighborhood. A putative finite maximal endpoint would have a state limit there, since its derivative is bounded; [F7] at that interior limit extends the solution, a contradiction. Thus it exists on the full interval. A finite subdivision and [F7] give smooth dependence on $\lambda$ throughout it. The unit timelike norm is preserved by [F8], and $\partial_0$ remains timelike on a smaller fixed tube for small $|\lambda|$, fixing the future cone.

Integrate the linearized equation twice, using $\delta s(u_1)=\partial_u\delta s(u_1)=0$, to obtain
$$\delta s^A(u_2)=\frac12\int_{u_1}^{u_2}(u_2-v)\,\partial_v^2H^A{}_B(v)\,s_0^B\,dv.$$
Integration by parts gives $\delta s^A(u_2)=\tfrac12[\Delta H^A{}_B-(u_2-u_1)\partial_uH^A{}_B(u_1)]s_0^B$. Since $H=C/r+\rho$, the endpoint condition $N_{AB}(u_1)=0$ and the $K_1r^{-2}$ bound give $\partial_uH(u_1)=O(r^{-2})$; the $K_0r^{-2}$ bound gives $\Delta H=\Delta C/r+O(r^{-2})$. This proves the stated displacement estimate, with constants depending on $u_2-u_1$ and $K_0,K_1$.

Integrating the linearized equation once gives $\partial_u\delta s^A(u_2)=\tfrac12(\partial_uH^A{}_B(u_2)-\partial_uH^A{}_B(u_1))s_0^B$. At both endpoints the leading derivative is $N^A{}_B/r=0$, and the $K_1r^{-2}$ bound controls the remainder derivatives. This proves the endpoint velocity estimate.

Smooth Gram-Schmidt at the initial point gives the chosen spatial orthonormal frame, since its projected Gram matrix is positive at $\lambda=0$ and remains positive nearby. Parallel transport solves $E'{}^a=-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}v^bE^c$, a linear equation with bounded smooth coefficients along the compact geodesic. Local solutions from [F7] extend over the interval: the equation gives $(|E|^2)'\le2C|E|^2$, so differentiating $e^{-2C(u-u_1)}|E|^2$ bounds $|E|$ by $|E(u_1)|e^{CT}$ and prevents escape at a finite endpoint, and local uniqueness patches a finite subdivision. They depend smoothly on $\lambda$ and remain orthonormal and orthogonal to the geodesic tangent by [F8]. The Jacobi initial-data result [F4] gives a unique field $J_\lambda$ with the stated covariant rest data. It is an actual variation field: choose an initial chart curve with tangent $J_\lambda(u_1)$, parallel-transport the initial timelike velocity along it, and issue geodesics from those data. The same compact-state argument as step 1.3 supplies the resulting smooth geodesic variation on the whole interval for sufficiently small variation parameter. Torsion-freeness gives initial covariant derivative zero, so uniqueness in [F4] identifies its variation field with $J_\lambda$.

Write $x_\lambda\in\mathbb R^3$ for the spatial components of $J_\lambda$ in that parallel frame; its time component is zero because $g(J_\lambda,\gamma_\lambda')$ is affine with zero initial value and derivative by [F4]. Its exact equation is
$$x_\lambda''=K_\lambda x_\lambda,\qquad (K_\lambda)^i{}_j=g_\lambda(E_{i,\lambda},R_\lambda(\gamma_\lambda',E_{j,\lambda})\gamma_\lambda'),\qquad x_\lambda(u_1)=x_0:=(s_0^1,s_0^2,0),\quad x_\lambda'(u_1)=0.$$
The coefficient is smooth jointly. At $\lambda=0$ the curvature vanishes identically, so curve and frame derivatives make no contribution to its first $\lambda$ derivative. The sign convention $R(T,J)T$ in [F4] and the positive $R^{(1)A}{}_{00B}=\tfrac12H''{}^A{}_B$ in [F3] give
$$K_\lambda=\lambda \mathcal K_1+\lambda^2L_\lambda,\qquad (\mathcal K_1)^A{}_B=\tfrac12H''{}^A{}_B,$$
with all first-order longitudinal entries zero. On a compact parameter interval $|\lambda|\le\delta_0$ one can take $L_\lambda=\int_0^1(1-t)\partial_\lambda^2K_{t\lambda}\,dt$, so $\|L_\lambda\|\le\ell$ uniformly on $[u_1,u_2]$. Put $\kappa:=\sup\|\mathcal K_1\|$ and $b:=\kappa+\delta_0\ell$.

Shrink $\delta\le\delta_0$ so $\delta T^2b/2\le1/2$. The exact integral equation
$$x_\lambda(u)=x_0+\int_{u_1}^{u}(u-v)K_\lambda(v)x_\lambda(v)\,dv$$
gives $\sup|x_\lambda|\le2|s_0|$ and $\sup|x_\lambda-x_0|\le T^2b|\lambda||s_0|$ for $|\lambda|\le\delta$. Define $x_1(u):=\int_{u_1}^{u}(u-v)\mathcal K_1(v)x_0\,dv$ and $e:=x_\lambda-x_0-\lambda x_1$. Subtracting the two integral equations yields
$$e(u)=\int_{u_1}^{u}(u-v)\left[\lambda \mathcal K_1(v)(x_\lambda(v)-x_0)+\lambda^2L_\lambda(v)x_\lambda(v)\right]dv.$$
Consequently
$$\sup|e|\le\frac{T^2}{2}(\kappa T^2b+2\ell)\lambda^2|s_0|,\qquad \sup|e'|\le T(\kappa T^2b+2\ell)\lambda^2|s_0|.$$
These are uniform bounds for this fixed family, tube and interval. The constants have respectively dimension zero and inverse length. No estimate in terms of $\sup|H|$ alone was used.

The screen part of $x_1$ is exactly $\delta s$ by step 1.2 and the zero initial data. Step 2.1 bounds
$$\left|\delta s(u_2)-\frac{\Delta C}{2r}s_0\right|\le\left(K_0+\frac{T K_1}{2}\right)r^{-2}|s_0|,$$
while step 2.2 bounds $|\delta s'(u_2)|\le K_1r^{-2}|s_0|$. Here $K_0,K_1$ are the profile-remainder constants from the Statement, distinct from the tidal matrix $\mathcal K_1$ in step 3.1. Combining with step 4.1 proves both quantitative endpoint formulas and their claimed uniformity. In particular, vanishing news at the two endpoints removes the leading $r^{-1}$ velocity response while retaining the stated finite-radius and amplitude errors. The estimate concerns the specified local normalized family only; it does not compare arbitrary finite-amplitude Bondi metrics to their plane-profile limit.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes u1<u2, so the interval is nonempty; step 1.1 uses those endpoints.
If N_AB=0, step 1.1 gives Delta C_AB=0; the detector displacement then has no leading term in step 2.1.

Let $c>0$ be a fixed conversion constant in metres per second. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of physical time in seconds, and let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ have dimensionless angular coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its quotient charts are local lifts to $\mathbb R^3$; chart changes are translations by elements of $(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Give $M=I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the product smooth structure, so $M$ is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Here a **$C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum** means a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ with $C^2$ components in smooth charts, whose value at each point has inertia $(3,1,0)$, together with a smooth vector field $N$ satisfying $g(N,N)<0$ everywhere. This is the explicit $C^2$ variant of the pointwise signature and time-orientation conditions in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; that supplier's metric regularity itself is smooth. Choose positive $C^2$ functions $a_i:I\to(0,\infty)$, $i=1,2,3$, with values in metres, and set

$$g=-c^2\,dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3a_i(t)^2\,(dx^i)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_t.$$

In every lifted product chart, $g$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-c^2,a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)$, so it is symmetric, $C^2$, and has inertia $(3,1,0)$; $N$ is smooth and $g(N,N)=-c^2<0$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ is a $C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum in the stated sense. This diagonal, spatially homogeneous metric datum is called a diagonal Bianchi I datum here; homogeneity means its coefficients are independent of the torus coordinates, and no isotropy is required. Define the directional expansion rates, their mean, the spatial volume scale and the squared directional shear by

$$H_i:=\frac{\dot a_i}{a_i},\qquad H:=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3H_i,\qquad V:=a_1a_2a_3,\qquad \sigma^2:=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^3(H_i-H)^2.$$

Here $\dot a_i=d a_i/dt$; $H_i$ and $H$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $V$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3$, and $\sigma^2$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The symbol $\sigma^2$ denotes a nonnegative scalar defined by this formula, not a tensor norm on a spacetime frame. This is a geometric ansatz and makes no field-equation or observational claim. The product and quotient constructions carry the inherited axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and use no stronger choice principle.

The local connection and Ricci components for this $C^2$ metric are defined separately.

The metric arrays and their derivatives therefore agree, so the displayed connection and curvature arrays patch consistently over the quotient atlas. $$R_{0i0i}=R_{i0i0}=-a_i^2(\dot H_i+H_i^2),\qquad R_{0ii0}=R_{i00i}=a_i^2(\dot H_i+H_i^2),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=-\sum_{i=1}^3(\dot H_i+H_i^2),\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ii}=\frac{a_i^2}{c^2}(\dot H_i+H_iH_\Sigma),$$

Let $a_i(t)=A_i(t/t_0)^{p_i}$ on a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq(0,\infty)$, where $A_i>0$ are lengths in metres, $t_0>0$ is a time in seconds, and $p_i\in\mathbb R$ are dimensionless exponents. These $p_i$ are called Kasner exponents for this power-law branch; define their sums $P:=\sum_{i=1}^3p_i$ and $Q:=\sum_{i=1}^3p_i^2$. For a nonstatic datum, meaning that not all $p_i$ vanish, the geometric vacuum equation $\operatorname{Ric}=0$ in the $C^2$ curvature definition of this page holds exactly when $P=Q=1$. If all $p_i=0$, then the full curvature tensor vanishes, so the metric is flat in the curvature sense. These are exact statements about the specified finite-dimensional metrics; no singularity or generic cosmological conclusion follows.

For a diagonal Bianchi I datum, let $\Lambda$ be a constant in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}$ and let $Q_i:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous functions in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. Suppose the spatial diagonal equations

$$G^i{}_i+\Lambda=Q_i(t)\qquad(i=1,2,3;\ \text{no sum over }i)$$

hold, where $G^i{}_i$ is defined by the local $C^2$ curvature convention on this page. With $\Delta_{ij}:=H_i-H_j$ and $H_\Sigma:=3H$, subtracting the equations gives

$$\dot\Delta_{ij}+3H\Delta_{ij}=c^2\bigl(Q_i-Q_j\bigr).$$

If the diagonal source is isotropic, meaning $Q_1=Q_2=Q_3$, then $V\Delta_{ij}$ is constant for each pair, and there is a constant $C\ge0$ such that $\sigma^2=C\,V^{-2}$ throughout $I$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $\mathcal L$ have a chosen first-variation decomposition with Euler
functional $E_\phi$. If $E_\phi=0$ and both variations satisfy the
linearized equations, so $\delta_iE_\phi=0$, then $d_M\omega=0$. For a finite
oriented smooth singular four-chain $C$ with
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

Thus on-shell closure alone gives independence between cuts only when the
side flux vanishes.

For a fixed smooth two-parameter family of commuting variations, replace the
Lagrangian and its selected potential by

$$\mathcal L'=\mathcal L+d_M\mu,\qquad \theta'(\phi;\delta\phi) =\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)+\delta\mu(\phi;\delta\phi) +d_MY(\phi;\delta\phi),$$

where $\mu$ is a local spacetime three-form and $Y$ is a local spacetime
two-form linear in the variation. Then

$$\omega'-\omega =d_M\bigl(\delta_2Y(\delta_1\phi)-\delta_1Y(\delta_2\phi)\bigr).$$

Consequently, for a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$,
the integrated form changes by the integral of this two-form over
$\partial\Sigma$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be a specified finite-dimensional smooth solution manifold
with specified admissible variations and boundary conditions, and let
$\Omega$ be a smooth closed two-form on $\mathcal S$, obtained by restricting
an integrated form $\Omega_\Sigma$ from the chosen covariant variation data.
The pair $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ is **presymplectic** when $\Omega$ is allowed
to be degenerate. At $p\in\mathcal S$, its pointwise null space is
$$\ker\Omega_p:=\{v\in T_p\mathcal S:\Omega_p(v,w)=0 \text{ for every }w\in T_p\mathcal S\}.$$
A **presymplectic reduction** is defined here only when there is a specified
smooth Hausdorff manifold $\mathcal R$ and a surjective submersion
$q:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$ with connected fibers such that
$$\ker(dq_p)=\ker\Omega_p\qquad(p\in\mathcal S),$$
where $\ker(dq_p)$ consists of tangent vectors mapped to zero by the
differential. This condition makes the quotient fibers exactly the connected
directions annihilated by $\Omega$. The reduction further requires a smooth
closed nondegenerate two-form $\bar\Omega$ on $\mathcal R$ satisfying
$q^*\bar\Omega=\Omega$. For a smooth vector field $X$ and smooth function
$H$ on a specified phase space, the Hamiltonian convention is
$\iota_X\Omega=dH$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. For an open subset $U$ of a smooth manifold, the **thin path groupoid** $\Pi^{\mathrm{thin}}_1(U)$ is the category whose objects are the points of $U$ and whose morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are tagged triples $(x,y,[\gamma])$, where $[\gamma]$ is a thin-homotopy class of piecewise-smooth paths from $x$ to $y$; composition, identities, and inverses are those of Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-thin-path-quotient-groupoid]].

Under the assumptions of [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]], if two piecewise-smooth paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to U$ are thin-homotopic in the sense of [[def-gr-fx-thin-paths]], then $U_{\gamma_0}(1)=U_{\gamma_1}(1)$ in the fixed tetrad trivialization.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

In a category $\mathcal C$ ([[def-category]]), a morphism $f:A\to B$ is an
**isomorphism** if there is a morphism $g:B\to A$ with
$g\circ f=1_A$ and $f\circ g=1_B$. Such a $g$ is unique and is denoted
$f^{-1}$.

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism. A
category is **connected** when it is nonempty and any two objects can be joined
by a finite zigzag of morphisms, with successive arrows allowed to point in
either direction. In a groupoid this is equivalent to being nonempty and having
an isomorphism between every ordered pair of objects. Nonemptiness cannot be
dropped: the empty groupoid has an isomorphism between every ordered pair of its
objects, vacuously, and is not connected.

For categories $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ ([[def-category]]), a **covariant
functor** $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ assigns an object $FA$ to every object
$A$ and a morphism $Ff:FA\to FB$ to every $f:A\to B$, satisfying

$$F(1_A)=1_{FA},\qquad F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff.$$

The **identity functor** acts identically on objects and morphisms. For
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E$, the
**composite functor** $GF$ has $(GF)A=G(FA)$ and $(GF)f=G(Ff)$.

A **contravariant functor** from $\mathcal C$ to $\mathcal D$ means a covariant
functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal D$, using
[[def-opposite-category]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

derivations.claim: On the constant path the coefficient $\omega(\dot\gamma)$ is zero, so the unique solution is $U(t)=I$. If $\gamma$ is followed by $\delta$, solve on the two parameter intervals with the terminal value from the first interval as initial value for the second. The second solution is $U_\delta(t)U_\gamma(1)$, so uniqueness gives $U_{\delta*\gamma}(1)=U_\delta(1)U_\gamma(1)$.

Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Along each smooth segment the derivative is $\frac{d}{dt}(U^{\mathsf T}\eta U)=U^{\mathsf T}(-\omega^{\mathsf T}\eta-\eta\omega)U=0$ by [F4]; continuity across the finite segment endpoints gives $U(t)^{\mathsf T}\eta U(t)=\eta$ throughout. Since $\eta$ is nonsingular, each $U(t)$ is invertible.

Let $U(t)$ solve along $\gamma$. The matrix $V(s):=U(1-s)U(1)^{-1}$ starts at $I$ and, since $\dot{\bar\gamma}(s)=-\dot\gamma(1-s)$, satisfies $V'(s)=-\omega(\dot{\bar\gamma}(s))V(s)$. Hence uniqueness gives $U_{\bar\gamma}(1)=U(1)^{-1}$. By [F3], transport is independent of the representative of a thin class; [F1]–[F2] and the identities in steps 1.1–1.2 therefore give well-defined component maps on the thin path groupoid.

For $[\gamma]:x\to y$ and $[\delta]:y\to z$, the associated tangent arrows compose as $(E_zU_\delta E_y^{-1})\circ(E_yU_\gamma E_x^{-1})=E_zU_\delta U_\gamma E_x^{-1}=E_zU_{\delta*\gamma}E_x^{-1}$ by step 1.1. Constant paths give identity tangent maps, and reversed paths give inverse tangent maps by step 2.1. Thus the stated object and arrow assignments define a functor into $\mathcal T(U)$ by [F6], with arrows in the stated groupoid by [F5].

Put $\widetilde U(t)=\Lambda(\gamma(t))U(t)\Lambda(\gamma(0))^{-1}$. Differentiating and using $U'=-\omega(\dot\gamma)U$ gives $\widetilde U'(t)=(d\Lambda(\dot\gamma)\Lambda^{-1}-\Lambda\omega(\dot\gamma)\Lambda^{-1})\widetilde U(t)=-\omega'(\dot\gamma)\widetilde U(t)$ by the transformation law [F4]. Its initial value is $I$, so uniqueness identifies $\widetilde U$ with transport in the changed frame and gives the endpoint formula. Since $E'_x=E_x\Lambda(x)^{-1}$, the corresponding tangent map is frame independent:

$$E'_yU'_\gamma(1)(E'_x)^{-1}=E_yU_\gamma(1)E_x^{-1}.$$

This is a local frame covariance statement; it is a principal-bundle gauge action only when $\Lambda$ has the global extension required by the cited gauge-group definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use the unitary Fourier transform
$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$ on
$L^1\cap L^2$. Let $H_0=-\Delta$ be the self-adjoint multiplier
$\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$ with domain
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Put
$Q_0=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^3\langle \partial_j u,\partial_j v\rangle_{L^2}\quad(u,v\in Q_0),$$
where $\partial_j$ are weak derivatives. Then $q_0$ is dense, symmetric,
nonnegative, and closed; its associated self-adjoint operator is exactly $H_0$,
with $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\langle H_0u,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_0),\ v\in Q_0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.
Assume countable choice. If $f\in L^1\cap L^2$, its bounded continuous integral transform $\widehat f$ represents $\mathcal F_2f$ almost everywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

derivations.claim: Spherical coordinates give $$\|G_\kappa\|_1=\int_0^\infty r e^{-\kappa r}\,dr=\kappa^{-2},\qquad \|G_\kappa\|_2^2=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-2\kappa r}\,dr =\frac1{8\pi\kappa}.$$ Thus both norms are finite; the point value at the origin does not affect the $L^p$ class.

For $\rho=|\xi|>0$, [F1] and the elementary integral $\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(ar)\,dr=a/(\kappa^2+a^2)$ for $a>0$ give $$\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)=\frac1{2\pi\rho}\int_0^\infty e^{-\kappa r}\sin(2\pi\rho r)\,dr =\frac1{\kappa^2+4\pi^2\rho^2}.$$ At $\xi=0$, direct integration gives $\widehat G_\kappa(0)=\int_0^\infty r e^{-\kappa r}\,dr=\kappa^{-2}$, the same formula.

Put $M=\|G_\kappa\|_1>0$ and $A(x)=\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)|^2dy$. Tonelli and translation invariance [F2, F3] give $\int A(x)dx=M\|f\|_2^2$, so $A(x)<\infty$ for almost every $x$. For each such $x$, $\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)|dy\le(M+A(x))/2<\infty$ by $2t\le1+t^2$, so define $b(x)=\int G_\kappa(y)f(x-y)dy$. Expanding the nonnegative integral $\int G_\kappa(y)|f(x-y)-b(x)/M|^2dy$ gives $0\le A(x)-|b(x)|^2/M$, hence $|b(x)|^2\le M A(x)$. Integrating yields $\|G_\kappa*f\|_2^2\le M^2\|f\|_2^2$. Therefore convolution is defined almost everywhere and gives a bounded operator on $L^2$.

If $f$ is Schwartz, then $G_\kappa*f\in L^1$ by Fubini and translation invariance [F3], and lies in $L^2$ by step 2.2. Fubini in the ordinary Fourier integral gives the integral-transform identity $\widehat{G_\kappa*f}=\widehat G_\kappa\widehat f$. Since $G_\kappa*f\in L^1\cap L^2$, [F4] identifies its integral transform with its Plancherel transform almost everywhere; the same interface identifies $\widehat f$ with $\mathcal F_2f$ almost everywhere. Thus $\mathcal F_2(G_\kappa*f)=\widehat G_\kappa\mathcal F_2f$ as $L^2$ classes. Since $|\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)|\le\|G_\kappa\|_1$ by the integral definition of the Fourier transform, multiplication by $\widehat G_\kappa$ is bounded on $L^2$. Schwartz density and boundedness of convolution therefore extend the identity to all $f\in L^2$.

By [A1], $-\Delta$ is the multiplier $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$. Therefore $(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)^{-1}$ is the bounded inverse multiplier of $-\Delta+\kappa^2$; its product with the latter multiplier is $1$, and its range lies in the operator domain because $4\pi^2|\xi|^2/(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)\le1$. Step 3.1 identifies the same multiplier for convolution, so convolution is exactly $(-\Delta+\kappa^2)^{-1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H$ be separable complex Hilbert spaces, $H_0$ and $H$ self-adjoint operators on them, and $J:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H$ a bounded linear map. Write $E_{H_0}$ and $E_H$ for their spectral projection valued measures. The absolutely continuous subspace $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ consists of vectors $u$ for which the scalar measure $B\mapsto\|E_{H_0}(B)u\|^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure; $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ is its orthogonal projection. Define the two-space wave operators, when the pointwise strong limits exist on $\mathcal H_0$, by

$$\Omega_\pm(H,H_0;J):=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty} e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0),$$

where a strong limit means that for every $u\in\mathcal H_0$ the vector-valued expression converges in $\mathcal H$. The two signs are separate limits. When $J=I$ and $\mathcal H_0=\mathcal H$, write $\Omega_\pm(H,H_0)$. A wave operator is complete when its range is all of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$. When both wave operators exist and are isometries on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$, the scattering operator on that subspace is

$$S(H,H_0;J):=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

When both are complete with common range $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$, $S$ is unitary. For a fixed finite number $r\ge1$ of channels on an open energy interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, finite-channel data additionally consists of the standard space $\mathbb C^r$ and a matrix field $S:I\to U(r)$, where

$$U(r):=\{U\in M_r(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_r\}.$$

Here $U^*$ is conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{tr}U=\sum_{j=1}^r U_{jj}$, and $\det U$ is the usual alternating determinant. The fixed channel number means that $I$ contains no channel threshold. This finite-channel data is an explicit on-shell input; the abstract wave-operator definition alone does not assert that a given pair has finite-dimensional energy fibers.

derivations.claim: Differentiating $S(E)^*S(E)=I_r$ entrywise gives $S'(E)^*S(E)+S(E)^*S'(E)=0$. Thus $A:=S^*S'$ satisfies $A^*=-A$, and $Q^*=(-i\hbar A)^*=i\hbar A^*=-i\hbar A=Q$.

Since $S$ is unitary, $S^{-1}=S^*$ and $\det S\ne0$. Multilinearity of the alternating determinant gives $\det(I_r+hA+o(h))=1+h\operatorname{tr}(A)+o(h)$ for $A=S(E)^{-1}S'(E)$: terms linear in $h$ are exactly the $r$ choices of one diagonal entry, while every nonidentity permutation or two off-diagonal factors contributes $o(h)$. Applying this to $S(E+h)=S(E)(I_r+hS(E)^{-1}S'(E)+o(h))$ yields $(\det S)'(E)=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^{-1}S'(E))=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^*S'(E))$. Multiplication by $-i\hbar/\det S(E)$ proves the trace formula.

For constant unitary $U_{\mathrm{in}},U_{\mathrm{out}}$, differentiation gives $(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{out}}^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, while $(S^\sharp)^*=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*U_{\mathrm{out}}$. Therefore $(S^\sharp)^*(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, proving the stated conjugation rule. Energy-dependent basis changes introduce derivatives of the basis matrices, so they are not covered by this claim.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

derivations.claim: Fix $x_0\in M$ and choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $\operatorname{ran}P(x_0)$. The vectors $P(x)e_j$ depend $C^2$ on $x$. Their Gram matrix is the identity at $x_0$, so its determinant remains positive on a neighborhood of $x_0$; hence the vectors remain linearly independent there. Applying the finite Gram–Schmidt formulas uses only sums, products, division by positive norms, and square roots of positive functions, so it gives a $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V(x)=(v_1(x),\ldots,v_r(x))$ for $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ on that neighborhood. The local bundle chart is $\Phi(x,z)=(x,V(x)z)$, with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(x,v)=(x,V(x)^*v)$; both maps are $C^2$. On an overlap, the frame change is $z\mapsto V_\beta(x)^*V_\alpha(x)z$, a $C^2$ map into the invertible complex matrices, so the transition maps are $C^2$. These charts make $E_P$ a rank-$r$ $C^2$ complex vector bundle. For $r=0$ the bundle is the zero bundle, and for $r=d$ every $P(x)=I_d$ and the bundle is trivial.

Along $\gamma$, abbreviate $P_\gamma$ by $P$. Differentiating $P^2=P$ gives $P'P+PP'=P'$ and $PP'P=0$. Therefore $K=P'P-PP'$ is $C^1$, $K^*=-K$, and $[K,P]=P'P+PP'=P'$. Let $M_K=\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|K(t)\|$, set $V_0(t)=I_d$, and recursively set $V_{n+1}(t)=\int_0^tK(u)V_n(u)\,du$. Induction gives $\|V_n(t)\|\leq(M_Kt)^n/n!$, so $W=\sum_{n=0}^\infty V_n$ converges uniformly and satisfies $W(t)=I_d+\int_0^tK(u)W(u)\,du$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $W'=KW$; since $K\in C^1$, also $W\in C^2$. If $Z$ is the difference of two solutions, iteration of $Z(t)=\int_0^tK(u)Z(u)\,du$ gives $\|Z(t)\|\leq\sup_{[0,1]}\|Z\|(M_Kt)^n/n!$ for every $n$, whose right side tends to zero, so $Z=0$.

abla(fs)=P\,d(fs)=P(df\,s+f\,ds)=df\,s+f
abla s$, so $
abla$ satisfies the connection Leibniz rule. For two such sections $s,t$, $d(s^*t)=(P\,ds)^*t+s^*(P\,dt)$ because $P=P^*$ and $Ps=s$, $Pt=t$; thus $

derivations.claim: The two parenthesizations of a triple product in $G_d$ have the same central coordinate, since both give $\theta+\theta'+\theta''-v'\cdot a-v''\cdot a-v''\cdot a'$. The identity is $(0,0,0)$ and the inverse of $(a,v,\theta)$ is $(-a,-v,-\theta-v\cdot a)$. Multiplying by $(0,0,\eta)$ on either side adds $\eta$ to the central coordinate and leaves $(a,v)$ fixed, so $Z$ is central; the quotient forgets $\theta$ and is the additive group $\mathbb R^{2d}$. The product and inverse maps are continuous in the product Euclidean topology: their coordinates are sums and the polynomial expression $\theta+\theta'-v'\cdot a$ or $-\theta-v\cdot a$. Thus $G_d$ is a topological group.
By [A2] and [F1], $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx;\mathbb C)$ with the stated pairing is a complex Hilbert space, so the operator definitions act on the required Hilbert space.

Translation is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes by [F2], and $\|T(a)f\|_2^2=\int |f(x-a)|^2dx=\int |f(x)|^2dx$ by [F3]. The map is linear with inverse $T(-a)$; hence it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.

The multiplier $e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}=\exp(imv\cdot x/\hbar)$ is continuous, hence measurable, by [F15], and has modulus one by [F16]. Therefore $B_m(v)$ preserves the norm. It is linear, and the addition law [F14] gives $B_m(v)B_m(-v)=I$; hence $B_m(-v)$ is its inverse and it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.

For almost every $x$, $(B_m(v)T(a)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}f(x-a)$ while $(T(a)B_m(v)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot(x-a)/\hbar}f(x-a)$. By the addition law [F14], $e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}=e^{imv\cdot(x-a)/\hbar}e^{imv\cdot a/\hbar}$, proving the commutation identity. Multiplying it on the right by $B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$ gives the displayed loop identity.

Let $g=u+iw\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$. For the unitary families established in steps 2.1 and 2.2, [F10] gives $u,w\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$; applying [F9] to each component and using $\|h+ik\|_2^2=\|h\|_2^2+\|k\|_2^2$ yields $\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2\to0$ as $a\to a_0$. If $v_n\to v_0$, continuity of the scalar exponential [F15] gives pointwise convergence $|e^{im(v_n-v_0)\cdot x/\hbar}-1|^2|g(x)|^2\to0$; by [F16] and the triangle inequality [F4], this is bounded by $4|g(x)|^2$, which is integrable. Dominated convergence [F12] gives $\|B_m(v_n)g-B_m(v_0)g\|_2\to0$. Since Euclidean parameter spaces are metric, both orbit maps are continuous on this dense smooth subspace.

For arbitrary $f\in\mathcal H$, approximate it in $L^2$ by $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ using [F8]. Unitarity in steps 2.1 and 2.2 gives $\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2\le2\|f-g\|_2+\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2$, and the analogous estimate for $B_m(v)$; letting the approximation error be arbitrarily small extends both continuities to every $f$. The scalar phase $e^{im\theta/\hbar}$ is continuous in $\theta$ by [F15]. Moreover,
$$\|\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)f-\Pi_m(a_0,v_0,\theta_0)f\|_2\le |e^{im\theta/\hbar}-e^{im\theta_0/\hbar}|\|f\|_2+\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2+\|(B_m(v)-B_m(v_0))T(a_0)f\|_2,$$
so the orbit map of $\Pi_m$ is norm-continuous on the product Euclidean group.

Using $T(a)B_m(v')=e^{-imv'\cdot a/\hbar}B_m(v')T(a)$ from step 3.1 and the translation law together with the exponential addition law [F14], multiplication gives $\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)\Pi_m(a',v',\theta')=\Pi_m(a+a',v+v',\theta+\theta'-v'\cdot a)$. By step 1.1 this is the group law; the operators are unitary by steps 2.1 and 2.2, and their orbit maps are continuous by step 4.1. Thus $\Pi_m$ is a unitary representation by [F5], and $\Pi_m(0,0,\eta)=e^{im\eta/\hbar}I$ is its central character.

For a finite direct sum the central subgroup acts as $\bigoplus_j e^{im_j\eta/\hbar}I_j$. If $m_j\ne m_k$, equality of the two central characters as functions would imply $\exp(im_j\eta/\hbar)=\exp(im_k\eta/\hbar)$ for every real $\eta$. By [F13], $\exp(0)=1$; by the derivative at zero from [F15], for every nonzero real $\alpha$ we have $\lim_{\eta\to0}(\exp(i\alpha\eta)-1)/\eta=i\alpha$, since factoring $i\alpha$ reduces this limit to the complex derivative of $\exp$ at $0$. Applying this with $\alpha=m_j/\hbar$ and $\alpha=m_k/\hbar$ would give $im_j/\hbar=im_k/\hbar$, contrary to $m_j\ne m_k$. Therefore the central characters are pairwise distinct.

Substituting $p=mv$ into the displayed Weyl formula gives $W(a,mv)=e^{-imv\cdot a/(2\hbar)}B_m(v)T(a)$. Direct multiplication, using the exponential addition law [F14], gives $W(a,p)W(a',p')=e^{-i\omega((a,p),(a',p'))/(2\hbar)}W(a+a',p+p')$. The published model result [F7] verifies this system is irreducible and regular, and [F6] gives unitary equivalence for every other system with the same finite phase space and nonzero parameter $1/\hbar$.

Then $\Phi_t$ is a finite quantum channel. The family $t\mapsto\Phi_t$ need not obey the semigroup law and need not be CP-divisible. The terms “semigroup law” and “CP-divisible” have the definitions of [[def-nrqmx-finite-channel-families]].

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a family of finite quantum channels indexed by $t\geq0$, where “finite quantum channel” has the meaning in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. The family obeys the **semigroup law** when $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{M_d(\mathbb C)}$ and $\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s$ for every $s,t\geq0$.

The family is **CP-divisible** when for every $0\leq s\leq t$ there exists a finite quantum channel $V_{t,s}:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi_t=V_{t,s}\circ\Phi_s$. CP-divisibility is this specified factorization property; the definition does not assert that it is a universal meaning of “Markovian”.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: In the environment $Z$ eigenbasis $|b\rangle$, $b=\pm1$, the finite spectral calculus [F7] gives $U_t=\sum_{b=\pm1}V_b(t)\otimes|b\rangle\langle b|$ with $V_b(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ibgt},e^{ibgt})$. By [F4], each diagonal phase has modulus one, so these blocks and $U_t$ are unitary. The environment state has equal weight on $b=\pm1$, so the reduced map is $\Phi_t(X)=\frac12(V_{+1}XV_{+1}^*+V_{-1}XV_{-1}^*)$; multiplying the two diagonal matrices shows that the off-diagonal entries are multiplied by $\kappa(t)=\frac12(e^{-2igt}+e^{2igt})=\cos(2gt)$, while the diagonal entries are unchanged.

By [F3] choose $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ with $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=1$, and put $s=\theta/(2g)>0$. Then [F4] gives $e^{i\theta}=i$, while [F5] and [F6] with $e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=e^0=1$ give $e^{-i\theta}=-i$; another application of [F5] yields $\kappa(s)=0$ and $\kappa(2s)=\frac12(e^{-2i\theta}+e^{2i\theta})=-1$.

Let $X_P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\rho_\pm=(I\pm X_P)/2$. Since $X_P=X_P^*$, $X_P^2=I$, and $\operatorname{Tr}X_P=0$, each $\rho_\pm$ is a positive trace-one matrix. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 give $\Phi_s(\rho_+)=\Phi_s(\rho_-)=I/2$, but $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)=\rho_-$ and $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_-)=\rho_+$. Thus $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)\ne\Phi_s(\Phi_s(\rho_+))$, so the semigroup law in [F2] fails. If a channel $V_{2s,s}$ satisfied $\Phi_{2s}=V_{2s,s}\circ\Phi_s$, it would map the equal intermediate states to equal outputs, contradicting their distinct final states; by [F1], every $\Phi_t$ is a channel, so the family is not CP-divisible by [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

$$\big(S_\lambda(q,p,t)f\big)(x) =e^{i\lambda t+i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q).$$
Then $S_\lambda$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]], has central character $t\mapsto e^{i\lambda t}$, and its Weyl operators form an irreducible regular Weyl system with phase $e^{-i\lambda\omega/2}$.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad
L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad
D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;
2. conversely, if $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb C$ is nonempty and compact and $E$ is
   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of
   $\Lambda$, then $T_E:=\int z\,dE(z)=\Phi_E(z)$ is a bounded normal operator
   with $\sigma(T_E)\subseteq\Lambda$ and $\|T_E\|\le\max_{z\in\Lambda}|z|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The formula for $W$ is a unitary composition of translation and a
modulus-one multiplier; its inverse is $W(-q,-p)$. Direct substitution gives
$$W(q,p)W(q',p')=e^{-i\hbar(q\cdot p'-p\cdot q')/2}W(q+q',p+p').$$
For a real symmetric $X$, the chirp
$$[C_Xf](x)=e^{ix^TXx/2}f(x)$$
is unitary, and substitution in the Weyl formula gives
$C_X^*W(q,p)C_X=W(q+Xp,p)$, the upper shear. For invertible real $A$,
$$[D_Af](x)=|\det A|^{1/2}f(Ax)$$
is unitary by [F5] applied to the diffeomorphism $x\mapsto Ax$ and the
integrable function $|f|^2$; direct
substitution gives
$D_A^*W(q,p)D_A=W(A^{-T}q,Ap)$, an invertible coordinate change.

Let $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$ be the exact angular-frequency unitary of
[F3]. Substitution into the Fourier integral on Schwartz functions gives
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}W(q,p)f](k)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,p\cdot(k-\sqrt\hbar q/2)}[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k-\sqrt\hbar q),$$
which is exactly $[W(p,-q)\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)$. Both sides are
bounded operators, and Schwartz functions are dense, so this identity holds
on all of $L^2$. Applying it to selected coordinates gives partial Fourier
rotations. Conjugating an upper shear by the full or partial
Fourier rotation gives every lower shear, since the matrix identity is
$\begin{pmatrix}0&-I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}
U_X\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}=L_{-X}$.
Thus each generator and inverse in [F2] has a unitary Weyl implementer.

Each generator unitary maps Schwartz space onto itself: this follows from
the product rule for the smooth quadratic chirp, the chain rule for an
invertible linear coordinate change, and Fourier invariance of Schwartz
space. On any connected parameter neighborhood on which $A$ remains
invertible, the chirp and coordinate formulas vary continuously in every
Schwartz seminorm; the Fourier factor is fixed. If
$G_1^*W(z)G_1=W(T_1z)$ and $G_2^*W(z)G_2=W(T_2z)$, then
$(G_1G_2)^*W(z)(G_1G_2)=W(T_2T_1z)$. Therefore, for any finite factorization
$T=T_k\cdots T_1$ supplied by [F2], multiplying the corresponding generator
unitaries in the order $G_1\cdots G_k$ gives a unitary $M_T$ with
$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)$ for every label $z$. This proves existence and does not
invoke a general metaplectic existence theorem.

Suppose $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $T$. Then
$X=M_2M_1^*$ commutes with every $W(z)$ by applying their two covariance
identities. Since the Weyl system is irreducible by [F1], every spectral
projection of either bounded self-adjoint operator
$\operatorname{Re}X=(X+X^*)/2$ and
$\operatorname{Im}X=(X-X^*)/(2i)$ commutes with every $W(z)$ and has invariant
range. Irreducibility forces each such projection to be $0$ or $I$. The
spectral measure in [F4] then implies each self-adjoint part is scalar: if a
bounded self-adjoint operator had two distinct spectral values, disjoint
neighborhoods of those values would yield a nonzero proper spectral
projection. Hence $X=\lambda I$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$; since $X$ is
unitary, $|\lambda|=1$. Thus $M_1,M_2$ differ only by a phase.

Give $\mathbb C^r$ the inner product $\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^r}=\sum_{a=1}^r\overline{v_a}w_a$, conjugate-linear in the first variable, and set $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d;\mathbb C^r)$ with

$$\langle\psi,\phi\rangle_{\mathcal H}:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\langle\psi_n,\phi_n\rangle_{\mathbb C^r}.$$

Let $\mathbb T^d_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $(2\pi)^{-d}dk$ and orientation $dk_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dk_d$, and set $\mathcal K=L^2(\mathbb T^d_{2\pi};\mathbb C^r)$ with

$$\langle f,g\rangle_{\mathcal K}:=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb T^d_{2\pi}}\sum_{a=1}^r\overline{f_a(k)}g_a(k)\,dk.$$

Thus the target pairing, like the sequence-space pairing, is conjugate-linear in its first variable. On finitely supported $\psi\in\mathcal H$ define

$$ (H_0\psi)_n=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta\psi_{n-\delta}. $$

On finitely supported sequences define

$$ (\mathcal F_0\psi)(k)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\psi_n e^{-ik\cdot n},\qquad h(k)=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta e^{-ik\cdot\delta}. $$
