derivations.claim: Direct multiplication of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\delta_{ab}I+i\sum_c\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$, $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_a=0$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\sigma_b)=2\delta_{ab}$. Thus $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=|n|^2I=I$, and $h=d_0I+|d|(n\cdot\sigma)$ has eigenvalues $d_0\pm|d|$ with the stated orthogonal projectors. Since $|d|$ is continuous and positive on compact $\mathbb T^2$, its minimum is positive, so the two bands are uniformly separated; $n$ and $P_s$ are smooth.

Differentiating $P_s=(I+s n\cdot\sigma)/2$ gives $\partial_jP_s=(s/2)(\partial_jn)\cdot\sigma$. The Pauli product identity yields $[a\cdot\sigma,b\cdot\sigma]=2i(a\times b)\cdot\sigma$, hence $[\partial_1P_s,\partial_2P_s]=\frac{i}{2}(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\cdot\sigma$. Using $\operatorname{tr}(P_s\sigma_a)=s n_a$, which follows from the trace identities in step 1.1, we obtain $\operatorname{tr}(P_s[\partial_1P_s,\partial_2P_s])=\frac{i s}{2}n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)$. In dimension two this is the coefficient of $\operatorname{tr}(P_s(dP_s\wedge dP_s)P_s)$: cyclicity and $P_s^2=P_s$ give $\operatorname{tr}(P_sXP_s)=\operatorname{tr}(P_sX)$. Multiplying by $i/(2\pi)$ therefore gives $C(P_s)=-s(4\pi)^{-1}\int n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\,dk_1dk_2$.

The normalized area form in [F3] pulls back to $(4\pi)^{-1}n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\,dk_1\wedge dk_2$, by the defining outward area form on the unit sphere. Hence its integral is $\deg(n)$ by [F3]. Substitution into step 2.1 gives $C(P_s)=-s\deg(n)$, which is the two displayed upper- and lower-band formulas.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth $n$-manifold without boundary. In a smooth chart $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, a smooth density is written $\phi_x(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. On a coordinate change $y=\psi(x)$ its coefficient transforms by
$$ \phi_y(y)=\phi_x(\psi^{-1}(y))\,|\det D\psi^{-1}(y)|. $$
A compactly supported smooth density is one whose support is compact in $M$. Give their space $\mathcal D(M;|\Lambda^nT^*M|)$ the locally convex test-density topology obtained from the usual fixed-compact derivative seminorms in charts and the corresponding LF inductive limit. A scalar distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test-density space, with bilinear pairing $\langle u,\omega\rangle$. Write $\mathcal D'(M)$ for these distributions and $\mathcal E'(M)$ for those with compact support. On a product manifold use the same definition with product densities. In a chart this definition is the ordinary distribution definition on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$; the displayed Jacobian law is the coordinate compatibility condition.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, using the local distribution convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. For $p\in\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, call $(p,\xi)$ regular for $u$ if there are $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\chi=1$ near $p$ and an open cone $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ containing $\xi$ such that for every integer $N\ge0$,
$$ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}(1+|\eta|)^N\left|\left\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|\right\rangle\right|<\infty. $$
The local wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_\Omega(u)$ is the complement of these regular pairs in $T^*\Omega\setminus0$, with the standard cotangent coordinates $(p,\xi)$. A cone is invariant under multiplication by positive scalars. This is a chart-level definition; this item makes no assertion about its behavior under a change of coordinates.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. Here $g$ is a smooth symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each tangent space with one negative and $n-1$ positive directions; in charts its signature is $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in each tangent space. A time orientation selects one of the two components of $\{v\ne0:g(v,v)<0\}$ as future. A tangent vector is causal when $g(v,v)\le0$, and is future or past causal when it belongs to the closure of the selected future or past timelike cone. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A nonzero cotangent vector is future or past causal, or future or past null, when its metric dual under $g^{-1}$ has the corresponding tangent property.

Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. It is coordinate-independent: under $y=\psi(x)$, $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det g_y|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det g_x|^{1/2}$, the density transformation law. Functional-kernel pairings and contractions on this page use $\mu_g$ in each integrated variable; no physical units are assigned.

For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. Two nonzero future-null cotangent vectors $(p,\xi)$ and $(q,\zeta)$ are related, written $(p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta)$, if $p=q$ and $\zeta=\xi$, or if there are a nonconstant future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic $\gamma:I\to M$, parameters $s,t\in I$ in either order, and a common scale $\lambda>0$ such that
$$p=\gamma(s),\qquad q=\gamma(t),\qquad \xi=\lambda g_p(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot),\qquad \zeta=\lambda g_q(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot).$$
These covectors are the metric-dual tangents to that geodesic and are related by induced covector parallel transport. There is no requirement $s\le t$: the future-frequency choice concerns the covectors, not an ordering of the two base points. The coincident case includes every nonzero future-null covector with $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. Write $W^{\mathsf T}=\tau^*W$ for the pullback by $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$. A fixed antisymmetric part means the equality $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for one specified distribution $E$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

A complex-linear functional $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is a distribution if and only if, for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, there are an integer $m_K\ge0$ and a finite constant $C_K\ge0$ such that
$$|u(\varphi)|\le C_K p_{m_K}(\varphi)\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D_K).$$
The quantifiers are $\forall K\,\exists(m_K,C_K)$; no simultaneous selection of witnesses is asserted or needed. The equivalence holds in ZF.

Assume Countable Choice.  Let $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ have compact
support, let $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'$ be its canonical extension, and let
$\chi\in\mathcal D$ equal one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}v$.
Then $\mathcal F\widetilde v$ is the regular tempered distribution represented
by

$$V(\xi)=\left\langle v_x,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\right\rangle.$$

The function $V$ is independent of $\chi$, is smooth, and for every
multi-index $\alpha$ there are $C_\alpha,m_\alpha$ with
$|\partial^\alpha V(\xi)|\leq C_\alpha(1+|\xi|)^{m_\alpha}$.  Consequently
multiplication by $V$ is continuous on $\mathcal S$ and, by transpose, on
$\mathcal S'$ in both dual topologies.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, the map

$$x\longmapsto T_x\varphi,\qquad (T_x\varphi)(y)=\varphi(x-y),$$

is $C^\infty$ as a map from $\mathbb R^n$ to Schwartz space, with
$\partial_x^\gamma T_x\varphi=T_x(\partial^\gamma\varphi)$.  This clause holds
in ZF.

Assume Countable Choice for the following integral clause.  Let $r\geq1$ and
let $H:\mathbb R^r\to\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous in every Schwartz
seminorm.  Suppose each $\partial_y^\beta H(t,y)$ is jointly measurable and,
for every $\alpha,\beta$, there is $g_{\alpha\beta}\in L^1(\mathbb R^r)$ such
that

$$p_{\alpha\beta}(H(t))\leq g_{\alpha\beta}(t)$$

for almost every $t$.  Then
$G(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^r}H(t,y)\,dt$ belongs to $\mathcal S$, derivatives pass
under the integral, and every $u\in\mathcal S'$ satisfies

$$\left\langle u,\int H(t)\,dt\right\rangle =\int\langle u,H(t)\rangle\,dt.$$

All integrals in this clause are Lebesgue integrals.
If $(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ are smooth charts on $M$ with $p\in U\cap V$, then the coordinate change on cotangent-fiber coordinates is given by the inverse transpose Jacobian of $y\circ x^{-1}$ at $x(p)$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

derivations.claim: In a chart, localize $u$ by a cutoff $\chi$ and write $\widehat{\chi u}(\xi)=\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}|dx|\rangle$. The finite-order bound [F3] gives polynomial growth in $\xi$ by differentiating the test at most its fixed order; parameter derivatives multiply it by powers of $x$, which remain bounded on the fixed compact support. Difference quotients converge in each fixed-support test seminorm by the Taylor remainder bound, so pairing shows that $\widehat{\chi u}$ is smooth. This is also the localized Fourier transform in [F4].

Suppose $(p,\xi_0)$ is regular for $u$ in the $x$ chart, witnessed by a cutoff $\chi_x$ and an open cone $\Gamma_x$. Let $y=\psi(x)$ be a smooth coordinate change, restrict to a compact patch about $p$, and put $\eta_0=(D\psi(p))^{-T}\xi_0$. Shrink the patch and choose nested cones $\Gamma_0\Subset\Gamma_1\Subset\Gamma_x$ around $\xi_0$ and a target cone $V$ around $\eta_0$ so that $D\psi(x)^TV\subset\Gamma_0$ throughout the patch. Choose a target cutoff $\chi_y$ equal to one near $p$ and supported where $\chi_x=1$, using [F8]. The target localized Fourier value is the source distribution paired with $a_\eta(x)=\chi_y(\psi(x))|\det D\psi(x)|e^{-2\pi i\psi(x)\cdot\eta}$; because $\chi_x=1$ on its support this is also the pairing with $\chi_xu$. Fourier inversion [F5], passed through this compactly supported distribution by [F6], expresses the value as $\int\widehat{\chi_xu}(\xi)\widehat{a_\eta}(-\xi)\,d\xi$. The phase in $\widehat{a_\eta}(-\xi)$ is $2\pi(x\cdot\xi-\psi(x)\cdot\eta)$, with gradient $2\pi(\xi-D\psi(x)^T\eta)$. In the near-stationary region $|\xi-D\psi(x)^T\eta|\le c(|\xi|+|\eta|)$, for sufficiently small $c>0$, cone separation gives $\xi\in\Gamma_x$ and $|\xi|\asymp|\eta|$; there $\widehat{\chi_xu}(\xi)$ decreases faster than every power, while $|\widehat{a_\eta}(-\xi)|\le\|a_\eta\|_1$ is uniformly bounded, and the region has only polynomial volume in $|\eta|$. On the complementary region the phase gradient is bounded below by $c(|\xi|+|\eta|)$; repeated integration by parts gives arbitrary powers of joint decay for $\widehat{a_\eta}(-\xi)$. The polynomial bound [F3] for $\widehat{\chi_xu}$ then makes this part rapidly decreasing after integration. This proves regularity in the target chart.

Applying step 2.1 also to $\psi^{-1}$ proves equivalence of regularity in both charts, and [F7] gives exactly $\eta=(D\psi)^{-T}\xi$. Regularity is open because the same cutoff and a smaller cone work for nearby base points; positive rescaling of a covector does not change rapid decay. Hence its complement is closed and conic.

Suppose $\chi_1$ is a regularity witness for $u$ on an open cone $\Gamma$, and let $\rho\in C_c^\infty$ have support where $\chi_1=1$. If $\Gamma'$ is an open cone whose closure of directions on the unit sphere is contained in $\Gamma$, then $\widehat{\rho u}$ is rapidly decreasing on $\Gamma'$. Indeed, $\rho u=\rho(\chi_1u)$ and Fourier inversion gives $\widehat{\rho u}=\widehat\rho*\widehat{\chi_1u}$; passing the Schwartz integral through the compactly supported distribution uses [F6]. Repeated integration by parts makes $\widehat\rho$ rapidly decreasing, and [F3] bounds $\widehat{\chi_1u}$ polynomially. Choose an intermediate cone with closure of directions between those of $\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma$. In the convolution, for frequencies $\eta$ in this intermediate cone with $|\eta|\ge|\xi|/2$, the second factor is rapidly decreasing at frequency comparable to $|\xi|$. If $|\eta|<|\xi|/2$, then $|\xi-\eta|>|\xi|/2$; for the remaining frequencies, $\eta$ lies outside the intermediate cone and $|\eta|\ge|\xi|/2$, so angular separation gives $|\xi-\eta|\ge c(|\xi|+|\eta|)$ for some $c>0$. In these latter regions the first factor is rapidly decreasing, while [F3] bounds the other factor polynomially. These estimates give the arbitrary-power bound for $|\xi|\ge1$ on $\Gamma'$, and [F4] gives boundedness on bounded sets. The convolution is absolutely integrable by the same estimates, and [F9] justifies its Fourier-integral identity. Applying this cutoff transfer to a common $\rho$ for witnesses for $u$ and $v$, and intersecting their smaller cones, gives rapid decay for $\widehat{\rho(u+v)}=\widehat{\rho u}+\widehat{\rho v}$. This proves $\operatorname{WF}(u+v)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup\operatorname{WF}(v)$. For a diffeomorphism, step 2.1 gives the cotangent image inclusion for pullback; applying the same argument to $\psi^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion.

If $u$ is smooth, integration by parts in a compact chart cutoff gives rapid decay in every cone. Conversely, suppose $\operatorname{WF}(u)=\varnothing$ and fix a point $p$ in a chart. In dimension zero every distribution is locally a scalar function, so assume the chart dimension is at least one. Form the set of all open cones $\Gamma'$ for which there exist a regularity witness $(\chi,\Gamma)$ at $p$ with the closure of the directions of $\Gamma'$ on the unit sphere contained in $\Gamma$. This set covers the unit covector sphere: every direction has a witness by emptiness of the local wavefront set, and its open cone contains a smaller cone about that direction. Compactness gives a finite subcover $\Gamma'_1,\ldots,\Gamma'_m$. For each member of this finite family, take a corresponding witness $\chi_j,\Gamma_j$; finite choice suffices. Their witness cutoffs all equal one on a neighborhood of $p$. By [F8], choose one cutoff $\rho$ equal to one near $p$ and supported in the intersection of those neighborhoods. Step 3.2 shows that the single localization $\rho u$ has rapidly decreasing Fourier transform on each $\Gamma'_j$. Since these finitely many cones cover the unit sphere, $\widehat{\rho u}$ is rapidly decreasing in every direction: for each $N$, take the maximum of the finitely many cone bounds outside a bounded ball. Therefore every differentiated inverse Fourier integral is absolutely convergent and defines a smooth function. Fourier inversion [F5] and the pairing interchange [F6], applied after a cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}(\rho u)$, identify this function with the compactly supported distribution $\rho u$. Hence $u$ is smooth near $p$; as $p$ was arbitrary, it is smooth in every chart.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, write Euclidean space as $E_d=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with coordinates $x=(t,\mathbf x)$, and put $S_d=\mathcal S(E_d;\mathbb C)$ and $S_{d,n}=\mathcal S(E_d^n;\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, with $S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0$ is the one-point vector space with unit measure. A Schwinger hierarchy is a sequence $S=(S_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $S_0=1$ and each $S_n\in S_{d,n}'$; its moments on elementary tests are $\langle S_n,f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n\rangle$. The associated unital algebraic test algebra is $T_d=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ with concatenation multiplication, unit $1\in S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$, and involution $(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*=\overline f_n\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline f_1$ and $(c1)^*=\overline c1$. The moments define $\omega_S:T_d\to\mathbb C$ by linear extension. At $d=4$ this is the same four-dimensional algebra and moment convention used by the positive-tempered-moment definition.

Ordinary moment positivity means $\omega_S(1)=1$ and $\omega_S(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in T_d$. It is distinct from reflection positivity. Let $\vartheta(t,\mathbf x)=(-t,\mathbf x)$ and $E_{d,+}=\{(t,\mathbf x):t>0\}$. The positive-time polynomial algebra $T_{d,+}$ is the unital star subalgebra generated by tests in $C_c^\infty(E_{d,+};\mathbb C)$. Define the antilinear reflection $\Theta$ by $\Theta f=\overline{f\circ\vartheta}$ on degree one, $\Theta(c1)=\overline c1$, and $\Theta(ab)=\Theta(b)\Theta(a)$. Reflection positivity is $\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in T_{d,+}$. The same formula applies to finite-site test algebras with an involution exchanging the sites.

A regulated hierarchy is a family $S^\lambda=(S^\lambda_n)_{n\ge0}$ indexed by a nonempty directed set $(\Lambda,\preceq)$, where directed means every two indices have a common upper bound. A distributional continuum limit is a hierarchy $S$ such that for every fixed $n$ and every $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$, $\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle\to\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ as $\lambda$ advances in $\Lambda$. A limit contract records these pairings, the regulator family, and any additional uniform estimates; pointwise-in-$n$ convergence by itself asserts no uniform bound as $n$ varies.

For explicit comparison, define the Schwartz seminorm $P_k(\Phi)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le k}\sup_{x\in E_d^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\Phi(x)|$ on $S_{d,n}$. A per-order uniform continuity record is a choice, for each fixed $n$, of $r_n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $C_n\ge0$ such that $|\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle|\le C_nP_{r_n}(\Phi)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. A uniform-order bound is the stronger explicit condition that there exist fixed $s\in\mathbb N$ and $A,B,q>0$ with $|\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle|\le A B^n(n!)^q P_{sn}(\Phi)$ for every $n\ge1$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. This bound is recorded separately and is not inferred from distributional convergence or asserted equivalent to a corrected Osterwalder–Schrader regularity hypothesis.

For $\gamma(x)=Rx+a$ with $R\in O(d)$ and $a\in E_d$, define $(U_\gamma\Phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\Phi(\gamma^{-1}x_1,\ldots,\gamma^{-1}x_n)$. Euclidean invariance means $\langle S_n,U_\gamma\Phi\rangle=\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ for every such $\gamma$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. Permutation symmetry means invariance of the pairing under each permutation of its $n$ argument blocks. Clustering means that for every $n,m\ge1$, $f\in S_{d,n}$ and $g\in S_{d,m}$,

$$
\langle S_{n+m},f\otimes\tau_{ae_0}g\rangle\longrightarrow \langle S_n,f\rangle\langle S_m,g\rangle\quad(a\to+\infty),
$$

where $e_0=(1,\mathbf0)$ and $(\tau_{ae_0}g)(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=g(x_1-ae_0,\ldots,x_m-ae_0)$. This contract definition asserts neither existence of a regulated limit nor any of these additional properties.

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^p)$ and $v\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^q)$, and use the Schwartz seminorms $p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$. The iterated pairing

$$
w(\Phi):=u\!\left(x\mapsto v\!\left(y\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\right)\right),\qquad \Phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q}),
$$

defines a tempered distribution $w\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. It satisfies $w(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$ for Schwartz functions $\varphi,\psi$. It agrees with the distribution tensor product on compactly supported tests, is unique with these product values, and its finite iterates are associative.

Use the Schwartz spaces and their seminorm topologies of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]]. Put
$S:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$ and
$S_n:=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{4n};\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, and set
$S_0:=\mathbb C$. A tempered distribution in $S_n'$ means a continuous
complex-linear functional on $S_n$
as in [[def-tempered-distribution]]; its pairing with a test is bilinear.

For complex vector spaces $S$, let $S^{\otimes_{\rm alg} n}$ be the algebraic
tensor product, characterized by multilinear maps out of $S^n$, with
$S^{\otimes_{\rm alg}0}:=\mathbb C1$. Define the algebraic tensor test algebra
$$T(S):=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n},$$
where the direct sum consists of finite-support sequences. Its multiplication
is concatenation of tensor factors, extended bilinearly, and its unit is $1$
in degree zero. Its conjugate-linear involution is specified on elementary
tensors by
$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*:=\overline{f_n}\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline{f_1},\qquad (c1)^*=\overline c1.$$

For $f_j\in S$, the elementary tensor is evaluated against a distribution by
the test function
$$J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\prod_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j).$$
This is in $S_n$: for multi-indices split into four-coordinate blocks
$(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$, its Schwartz seminorm is
$$p_{(\alpha_j)_j,(\beta_j)_j}(J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n))=\prod_{j=1}^n p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f_j).$$
Thus $J_n$ is multilinear and continuous, and the displayed formula extends
linearly to the algebraic tensor product.
In degree zero set $J_0(c1):=c$.

By these definitions concatenation is associative with the degree-zero unit,
and reversal together with complex conjugation is an involution satisfying
$(ab)^*=b^*a^*$; thus $T(S)$ is a unital complex star algebra.

A **positive tempered moment family** is a sequence consisting of $W_0=1$
and $W_n\in S_n'$ for each $n\ge1$ such that the multilinear maps
$$f_1,\ldots,f_n\longmapsto\langle W_n,J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)\rangle$$
extend, degree by degree and then over finite sums, to a complex-linear
functional $\omega:T(S)\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\omega(1)=1,\qquad \omega(a^*a)\in[0,\infty)\quad(a\in T(S)).$$
Equivalently, the family supplies an actually positive normalized functional
on this algebra. Positivity is a hypothesis on the distributions; formal
coefficient families do not qualify merely because they obey algebraic
identities. No topology on $T(S)$, norm completion, C*-algebra, or existence
claim for an interacting field is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every real polynomial $P$ in $Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E|P(Q)|<\infty$, and its expectation $\mathbb E[P(Q)]$ is computed by expanding $P$ into monomials and applying finitely many covariance pairings.

Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], exactly as required by the
published Schwartz Fourier theorem.  For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$
put

$$\widehat\varphi(\xi)=\mathcal F\varphi(\xi) =\int_{\mathbb R^n}\varphi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$

For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ define its **Fourier transform** by

$$\langle\mathcal Fu,\varphi\rangle =\langle u,\mathcal F\varphi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).$$

The published automorphism
[[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]
sends Schwartz tests continuously to Schwartz tests, so composition with the
continuous functional of [[def-tempered-distribution]] is again a continuous
complex-linear functional.  Hence $\mathcal Fu\in\mathcal S'$.  The pairing
is bilinear: there is no conjugation and no inverse transform on the
right-hand side.  Countable Choice is used only through the cited published
Fourier construction; transposition itself uses no additional choice.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: The full Axiom of Choice assumed in [A1] implies Countable Choice: if $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is any sequence of nonempty sets, AC supplies a choice function $g$ on the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, and $n\mapsto g(X_n)$ chooses from every $X_n$. Thus the actual Countable Choice hypotheses of [F6] and [F7] are satisfied before those suppliers are used. The full Fourier transform $\widehat\Phi$ of $\Phi\in\mathcal S(E_d\times E_d)$ is Schwartz by [F6]. For $|p|<1$, its zero-weight seminorm bounds the value. A **multitensor category over $k$** is a locally finite $k$-linear abelian,
rigid monoidal category whose tensor product is $k$-bilinear in both variables.
A **tensor category** is a multitensor category for which
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)\cong k$ as $k$-algebras.

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided monoidal category and let $X$ be an object of
$\mathcal C$. Each **formal canonical composite** on $X^{\otimes n}$ built
from associators, unitors, braidings, and their inverses has an underlying
braid in $B_n$. If two such formal composites have equal underlying braids,
then their interpreted morphisms in $\mathcal C$ are equal. Different formal
braids may, of course, have the same interpretation in a particular braided
category.

For $n\ge2$, the **braid group** $B_n$ is the group with generators
$\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations

$$\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\qquad(1\le i\le n-2),$$

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

interpreted in the sense of [[def-group-presentation]] and
[[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]].

For $n=0$ and $n=1$, there are no generators, and $B_n$ is the trivial group
given by the empty presentation.

Let $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ be a presentation, let $H$ be a group, and let
$u:X\to H$ be a function. If the evaluation of every $r\in R$ under $u$ is
$e_H$, then there is a unique homomorphism

$$\overline u:\langle X\mid R\rangle\longrightarrow H$$

with $\overline u([x])=u(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Moreover, $\overline u$ is
surjective if and only if $u(X)$ generates $H$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field with bijective antipode, and let $(h_i)$ and $(f_i)$ be dual bases of $H$ and $H^*$. In the factor order $D(H)=H^{*\mathrm{op}}\otimes H$, the tensor

$$R=\sum_i(f_i\otimes1_H)\otimes(\varepsilon_H\otimes h_i)$$

is basis-independent and invertible, with

$$R^{-1}=\sum_i(f_i\otimes1_H)\otimes(\varepsilon_H\otimes S^{-1}(h_i)).$$

It is quasitriangular in the convention

$$R\Delta_D(d)=\Delta_D^{\mathrm{op}}(d)R,\qquad(\Delta_D\otimes\operatorname{id})R=R_{13}R_{23},\qquad\alpha^{-1}_{D,D,D}(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta_D)R=R_{13}R_{12}.$$

On every pair of left $D(H)$-modules, $\tau\circ R$ is the Yetter–Drinfeld braiding of [[thm-hh-double-modules-and-yetter-drinfeld-modules]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth three-manifold, possibly with smooth boundary, and fix a trivialization of a principal $G$-bundle over $M$, where $G$ has finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Give $\mathfrak g$ its Lie bracket $[\ ,\ ]_{\mathfrak g}$ and a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathfrak g}$ satisfying $\langle[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g},Z\rangle_{\mathfrak g}=\langle X,[Y,Z]_{\mathfrak g}\rangle_{\mathfrak g}$. Write $\Omega^p(M;\mathfrak g)=\Gamma(M,\wedge^pT^*M\otimes\mathfrak g)$ for smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $p$-forms. Extend the Lie bracket and pairing to homogeneous simple tensors by $[X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta]=[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g}\otimes(\alpha\wedge\beta)$ and $\langle X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta\rangle=\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathfrak g}\,\alpha\wedge\beta$, then extend bilinearly.

A connection in the chosen trivialization is a form $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$. Its curvature and covariant exterior derivative are $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A,A]$ and $D_AX=dX+[A,X]$. Define the local Chern–Simons functional and the BF functional, for $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, by

$$\operatorname{CS}(A)=\int_M\left\langle A\wedge dA+\tfrac13A\wedge[A,A]\right\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{BF}(B,A)=\int_M\langle B\wedge F_A\rangle.$$

These are integrals of smooth top forms on a compact oriented manifold. The Chern–Simons formula is the local expression in the fixed trivialization; it does not define a globally gauge-invariant exponentiated action on arbitrary nontrivial bundles without additional characteristic-class and level data. No path-integral measure, quantization, or identification with a Reshetikhin–Turaev amplitude is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth three-manifold with boundary, $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra with invariant nondegenerate symmetric pairing, and $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$ a smooth connection in a fixed trivialization. For an arbitrary smooth variation $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, the Chern–Simons first variation is

$$\delta\operatorname{CS}_A(\alpha)=2\int_M\langle\alpha\wedge F_A\rangle-\int_{\partial M}\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle,$$

where $\partial M$ has the outward-normal-first orientation. Thus the boundary term is part of the variation; the bulk Euler equation is $F_A=0$ when variations are compactly supported in $\operatorname{int}M$ (or when boundary data make the boundary variation vanish). For $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$ the BF action has first variation

$$\delta\operatorname{BF}_{(B,A)}(\beta,\alpha)=\int_M\langle\beta\wedge F_A\rangle+\int_M\langle\alpha\wedge D_AB\rangle-\int_{\partial M}\langle B\wedge\alpha\rangle,$$

so interior-compact variations give the equations $F_A=0$ and $D_AB=0$. No boundary condition is imposed by these bulk equations.

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ fixed, the boundary potential current of $\lambda\operatorname{CS}$ is $\theta_A(\alpha)=-\lambda\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle$. On a compact oriented smooth surface $\Sigma$ (with smooth boundary allowed), put $\mathcal A_\Sigma=\Omega^1(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$ and identify each tangent space with $\Omega^1(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$. For $a\in\mathcal A_\Sigma$ define $\Theta_\Sigma|_a(\alpha)=\int_\Sigma\theta_a(\alpha)$, and let $\Omega_\Sigma=d_{\mathcal A_\Sigma}\Theta_\Sigma$. The restriction to the flat-connection solution space, wherever it is smooth, is the possibly degenerate presymplectic form. Explicitly, on tangent vectors $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ it is the constant closed form

$$\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=-2\lambda\int_\Sigma\langle\alpha_1\wedge\alpha_2\rangle.$$

At a flat connection $a$ ($F_a=0$), tangent variations $\alpha$ to the flat-connection equations satisfy $D_a\alpha=0$. For an infinitesimal gauge parameter $\epsilon\in C^\infty(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$, the gauge direction is $D_a\epsilon$ and

$$\Omega_\Sigma(D_a\epsilon,\alpha)=-2\lambda\int_{\partial\Sigma}\langle\epsilon,\alpha\rangle.$$

Consequently gauge parameters vanishing on $\partial\Sigma$ generate null directions on the linearized flat locus. If $\epsilon$ is field-independent, the displayed boundary variation is $\delta Q_\epsilon$ for $Q_\epsilon(a)=-2\lambda\int_{\partial\Sigma}\langle\epsilon,a\rangle$. For $\lambda\ne0$, nonzero boundary parameters need not be null and can carry such charges when the boundary conditions permit them; no charge algebra or integrability assertion for field-dependent parameters is made. If $\lambda=0$, the displayed $\Theta_\Sigma$, $\Omega_\Sigma$ and $Q_\epsilon$ vanish identically, and every gauge direction on the linearized flat locus is null.

Let $V$ be a three-dimensional real vector space with Lorentzian inner product $g$ of signature $(-,+,+)$. Let $R_{abcd}$ be an algebraic curvature tensor: it is antisymmetric in $a,b$ and in $c,d$, symmetric under exchange of the pairs, and satisfies $R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}=0$. Define $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=g^{ac}R_{abcd}$ and $\operatorname{Scal}=g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$. Then

$$R_{abcd}=g_{ac}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}-g_{ad}\operatorname{Ric}_{bc}-g_{bc}\operatorname{Ric}_{ad}+g_{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{ac}-\tfrac12\operatorname{Scal}(g_{ac}g_{bd}-g_{ad}g_{bc}).$$

In particular, $\operatorname{Ric}=0$ if and only if $R_{abcd}=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space
with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in its first argument. Use
$p\cdot a:=p^0a^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf a$ on $\mathbb R^4$, the convention
of the proper-orthochronous Poincaré supplier, and put
$$\overline V_+:=\{p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in\mathbb R^4:p^0\ge|\mathbf p|\},\qquad
V_+:=\{b=(b^0,\mathbf b)\in\mathbb R^4:b^0>|\mathbf b|\}.$$
For estimates only, write
$|p|_{\mathrm E}:=\sqrt{(p^0)^2+|\mathbf p|^2}$.

Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^4$:
each $E(S)$ is an orthogonal projection, $E(\varnothing)=0$,
$E(\mathbb R^4)=I$, $E(S\cap T)=E(S)E(T)$, and for every disjoint sequence
$(S_n)$, $E(\bigcup_nS_n)\xi=\sum_nE(S_n)\xi$ in norm for each
$\xi\in\mathcal H$. For a bounded Borel function $g$, write
$\Phi_E(g):=\int g(p)\,dE(p)$ for its bounded spectral integral, defined by
uniform simple-function approximation. Let
$U:\mathbb R^4\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ be a strongly continuous unitary
representation of translations: $U(0)=I$, $U(a+a')=U(a)U(a')$, every $U(a)$
is a surjective linear isometry, and $a\mapsto U(a)\xi$ is norm-continuous for
each $\xi\in\mathcal H$. The **positive-energy joint spectral input** is the
additional data and condition
$$U(a)=\Phi_E\bigl(p\mapsto e^{ip\cdot a}\bigr),\qquad
E(\mathbb R^4\setminus\overline V_+)=0.$$

Fix a translation-invariant unit vector $\Omega\in\mathcal H$, so $U(a)\Omega=\Omega$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^4$, and a specified unital $*$-subalgebra
$\mathfrak A\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ such that
$\overline{\{A\Omega:A\in\mathfrak A\}}=\mathcal H$; this is the meaning of
cyclic vacuum here. If local bounded operators are used, their assignment
$O\mapsto\mathfrak A(O)\subseteq\mathfrak A$ for bounded open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ is separately specified. This input asserts no
locality, isotony, covariance, or field-domain property for that assignment.
The PVM and its joint support are input; separate generators or a
matrix-coefficient Fourier-support condition do not replace this additional
data.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-energy joint spectral input of
[[def-qftx-joint-spectrum-input]] on $\mathcal H$. Put
$\mathcal T_+:=\{a+ib:a\in\mathbb R^4,\ b\in V_+\}$ and, for
$z=a+ib\in\mathcal T_+$, define
$$U(z):=\Phi_E\bigl(p\mapsto\mathbf1_{\overline V_+}(p)e^{ip\cdot z}\bigr),
\qquad p\cdot z:=p^0z^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf z.$$
Then $U(z)$ is a bounded operator with $\|U(z)\|\le1$; the same formula
extends it to a strongly continuous contraction-valued map on
$\mathbb R^4+i\overline V_+$ and agrees with the given $U(a)$ when $b=0$.
Holomorphic means complex differentiable as a map of the full complex
coordinate vector, with a complex-linear total derivative and remainder
$o(\|h\|)$.

For every integer $n\ge1$, every $B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1}\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$,
and every $\psi,\phi\in\mathcal H$, the matrix coefficient
$$F(z_1,\ldots,z_n):=
\bigl(U(z_1)B_1U(z_2)\cdots B_{n-1}U(z_n)\psi,\phi\bigr)$$
is holomorphic on $\mathcal T_+^n$, where each
$\operatorname{Im}z_j\in V_+$. No locality assumption on the bounded
insertions is used. This result concerns bounded operators; it asserts no
domain, product, or holomorphy claim for unbounded Wightman fields.

For Borel sets $S,T$, $E_p(S)$ is diagonal with entries in $\{0,1\}$,
$E_p(\mathbb R^4)=I$, and
$E_p(S\cap T)=E_p(S)E_p(T)$. For a disjoint sequence, each of the distinct
points $0,p$ belongs to at most one set, so the coordinatewise sum of the
projections is $E_p(\bigcup_n S_n)$ and is finite on every vector. Thus $E_p$
is a strongly countably additive PVM supported on $\{0,p\}\subseteq\overline
V_+$. The diagonal operators $U_p(a)$ form a unitary representation because
$|e^{ip\cdot a}|=1$ and $U_p(a+a')=U_p(a)U_p(a')$; continuity is ordinary
continuity of the exponential. Put $P_0:=E_p(\{0\})=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$
and $P_p:=E_p(\{p\})=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. Since $p\ne0$, these are the
two spectral projections and $E_p$ vanishes off their supports. Therefore the
bounded Borel multiplier $q\mapsto e^{iq\cdot a}$ has integral
$$\Phi_{E_p}(q\mapsto e^{iq\cdot a})=e^{i0\cdot a}P_0+e^{ip\cdot a}P_p
=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{ip\cdot a})=U_p(a),$$
by the finite-support PVM integral formula. Also $U_p(a)\Omega=\Omega$. For every
$(x,y)\in\mathbb C^2$, the matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\y&0\end{pmatrix}$ sends $\Omega$ to $(x,y)$, so
$\Omega$ is cyclic for $\mathfrak A$.

The cone-restricted multiplier has values $1$ at $0$ and
$e^{ip\cdot(a+ib)}=e^{ip\cdot a}e^{-p\cdot b}$ at $p$; hence its PVM integral
is $\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{ip\cdot a-p\cdot b})$. For $b\in V_+$,
$p\cdot b\ge p^0(b^0-|\mathbf b|)>0$, since nonzero $p\in\overline V_+$
has $p^0>0$. Therefore the $e_1$ eigenvalue has modulus
$e^{-p\cdot b}<1$, while the $e_0$ eigenvalue is $1$. The operator norm is
$1$, in agreement with [F2].

On the $e_1$ component the reversed-sign continuation is
$e^{-ip\cdot(a+ib)}=e^{-ip\cdot a+p\cdot b}$, of modulus
$e^{p\cdot b}>1$ for $b\in V_+$. For $b\in -V_+$, $p\cdot b<0$, so its
modulus is less than $1$. The $e_0$ vacuum component stays $1$ in both
continuations. Thus the nonzero frequency's damping direction reverses with
the Fourier sign.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. All indices $n,N$ below range over $\mathbb N$. Fix $d\in\mathbb N$ with $d\geq1$, an even Borel pair potential $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with no $-\infty$ values, stable with constant $B\in\mathbb R$, $B\geq0$, and inverse parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R$ with $\beta>0$. Put $e^{-c(+\infty)}=0$ for every $c>0$, $f_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and $C_\beta=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty$. For each $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq2$, use

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j),$$

where $\mathcal C_n$ is the set of connected simple graphs on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; set $U_1=1$. For $L\in\mathbb R$ with $L>0$, let $\Lambda_L=[-L,L]^d$ and write $|\Lambda_L|:=\lambda_d(\Lambda_L)=(2L)^d$; define

$$\Xi_L(z):=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}v(x_i-x_j)\right)\,dx_1\cdots dx_N,$$

with the $N=0$ term equal to $1$. Set $b_1(L)=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n(L):=\frac1{n!|\Lambda_L|}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n.$$

Also set $b_1=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n:=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_2\cdots dx_n.$$

Let $\mathcal D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|e^{2\beta B+1}C_\beta<1\}$ when $C_\beta>0$, and let $\mathcal D=\mathbb C$ when $C_\beta=0$. On $\mathcal D$, the finite-volume connected pressure series $p_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_n(L)z^n$ and the limiting Mayer pressure series $p(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_nz^n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, are differentiable term by term, and satisfy

$$\Xi_L(z)=\exp\!\bigl(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)\bigr),\qquad \lim_{L\to\infty}p_L(z)=p(z).$$

The convergence and derivative limits are uniform on every compact subdisc of $\mathcal D$. The pressure limit here is along centered cubes only.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: The Euclidean norm is even by [F5], so $v_a(-x)=v_a(x)$. The ball $B(0,a)$ is open, hence Borel, by [F4]; its complement is Borel as well. The target singleton $\{+\infty\}$ is Borel by [F4], and $\{0\}=\bigcap_{m\geq1}(-1/m,1/m)$ is Borel by the extended-real topology and sigma-algebra closure in [F4]. Since $v_a$ takes the constant value $+\infty$ on the ball and $0$ on its complement, the preimage of any target Borel set is among the empty set, the ball, its complement, and all of $\mathbb R^d$; hence $v_a$ is Borel. Every pair energy is either $0$ or $+\infty$, so every finite total energy is at least zero; therefore the stability inequality holds with $B=0$.

Under the stated convention, $e^{-\beta v_a(x)}-1=-1$ on $B(0,a)$ and $0$ elsewhere, so $|f_\beta|=\mathbf1_{B(0,a)}$ by [F8]. The ball lemma [F3] gives measurability and finite measure, and [F6] gives $C_\beta=\int\mathbf1_{B(0,a)}dx=\lambda_d(B(0,a))\in(0,\infty)$.

The hypotheses of [F2] hold by steps 1.1–1.2 and [A1]. Substituting $B=0$ and $C_\beta=\lambda_d(B(0,a))$ into its sufficient disk gives $e|z|\lambda_d(B(0,a))<1$. This is a sufficient analytic domain; it is not asserted to be necessary and implies no freezing or coexistence point.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite, let $p$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$, and set $S:=\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{a\in\mathcal A:p(a)>0\}$. Then $S$ is finite nonempty and $p(a)>0$ on $S$. For each $n\ge1$, use the finite product law $p^{\otimes n}$ from [[def-it-finite-alphabet-product-law]] and [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]] on $\mathcal A^n$, and let $X_1^{(n)},\ldots,X_n^{(n)}$ be its coordinate maps. Let $\widehat P_n$ be the empirical type of this coordinate word, viewed as a $\Delta(\mathcal A)$-valued map. Identify the support simplex
$$\Delta(S):=\{q\in[0,1]^S:\sum_{a\in S}q(a)=1\}$$
with the face of $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ whose coordinates outside $S$ vanish. Then $\widehat P_n\in\Delta(S)$ almost surely under $p^{\otimes n}$. For any set $\Gamma\subseteq\Delta(S)$, let $\Gamma^\circ$ and $\overline\Gamma$ denote its interior and closure in the relative topology induced by $\|\cdot\|_1$.
With $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\ge-\inf_{q\in\Gamma^\circ}D(q\|p),$$
and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le-\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p).$$
For every $n\ge1$ the finite upper bound
$$p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le(n+1)^{|S|-1}\exp\!\left(-n\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p)\right)$$
also holds. If the two infima agree, the limit exists and equals their negative common value. Equivalently, when $S\ne\mathcal A$, one may restrict the product sample space to $S^n$ without changing these event probabilities, since every word outside $S^n$ has zero product mass.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and let $p$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$. Then $q\mapsto D(q\|p)$ is finite and continuous on the probability simplex $\Delta(\mathcal A)$.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim:
Enumerate $\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_d\}$, with $d\geq1$, and identify $\mathbb R^{\mathcal A}$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^d$. Write $\|x\|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^d|x_i|$ and $\|x\|_2:=(\sum_{i=1}^dx_i^2)^{1/2}$; the declared $\ell^1$ topology on the simplex is the topology from $\|\cdot\|_1$. The simplex is closed because it is the intersection of the closed coordinate constraints $0\leq q(a_i)\leq1$ and the closed affine constraint $\sum_iq(a_i)=1$; these are closed since coordinate maps and their finite sum are continuous. It is bounded because $\|q\|_2^2=\sum_iq(a_i)^2\leq\sum_iq(a_i)=1$. By [F6] it is compact in the Euclidean topology. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $\|x\|_2\leq\|x\|_1$ because $(\sum_i|x_i|)^2\geq\sum_ix_i^2$, and $\|x\|_1\leq d\|x\|_2$ because $\sum_i|x_i|\leq d\max_i|x_i|\leq d\|x\|_2$. These inequalities show that the Euclidean and $\ell^1$ metrics have the same open sets, so the simplex is compact in its declared topology. By continuity of $h$ and $D$, each fiber $h^{-1}(\{u\})$ and each sublevel set $\{q:D(q\|p)\leq r\}$ is closed in the simplex and hence compact by [F7]. The continuous-image and extreme-value conclusions in [F8] therefore apply to these sets. In particular, [F4] makes $q\mapsto D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)$ continuous on the compact simplex, so it attains a finite minimum $m_\beta$. The rate $D$ is nonnegative by [F5]. The empirical macrostate law under $p^{\otimes n}$ has rate $D(q\|p)$ by [F2]. For every Borel $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$, the canonical macrostate probability is exactly
$$p_{n,\beta}(L_n\in B)=\frac{\int_Be^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)}{\int_{\Delta(\mathcal A)}e^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)},$$
where $\mu_n$ is the base law of $L_n$; this follows by summing the word weights in [F1] over the fiber $L_n^{-1}(B)$. Thus it is the tilt in [F3] with $F=-\beta h$, and its rate is $D+\beta h-m_\beta$. Its zero set is $\mathcal M_\beta$. Let $U$ be any open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_\beta$ and put $C:=\Delta(\mathcal A)\setminus U$. If $C=\varnothing$, the probability of the complement is zero. Otherwise $C$ is a nonempty closed subset of the compact simplex, hence compact by [F7]. The continuous rate is positive at every point of $C$ because its zero set is $\mathcal M_\beta\subset U$; by [F8] it attains a strictly positive minimum on $C$, and the LDP upper bound makes the canonical macrostate probability of that complement exponentially small.

The fiber $H_u:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u\}$ is nonempty and closed, hence compact by step 1.1 and [F7], because $u$ is in the range of continuous $h$. By [F4] and [F8], $D$ attains its finite minimum $d(u)$ on $H_u$, so $\mathcal M_u$ is nonempty. For fixed $\delta>0$, put $B_\delta:=\{q:|h(q)-u|<\delta\}$; it is open and contains $H_u$. By [F2],
$$-\inf_{B_\delta}D\leq\liminf_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq\limsup_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq-\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D.$$
For each matching radius $\delta_j$ in the Statement the two infima agree, so the inner limit exists and equals their negative common value. The lower bound is finite because $B_{\delta_j}$ contains a finite-rate point of $H_u$; hence the conditioning event has positive probability for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $q\in\mathcal M_\beta$ and put $u=h(q)$. If $r\in H_u$, then $D(r)+\beta u\geq D(q)+\beta u$, so $q\in\mathcal M_u$ and $D(q)=d(u)$. For any $v$ in the energy range, minimizing over $H_v$ gives $d(v)+\beta v\geq d(u)+\beta u$, equivalently $s(v)-\beta v\leq s(u)-\beta u$. Thus $u$ maximizes the stated entropy-minus-energy expression.

Write $d_\delta:=\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D$ for any $\delta>0$; since $H_u\subseteq\overline B_\delta$, $d_\delta\leq d(u)$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and let $K_\varepsilon:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):D(q\|p)\leq d(u)-\varepsilon\}$. By [F4], this set is closed and hence compact by [F7]; it is disjoint from $H_u$ by the definition of $d(u)$. Thus its compact image $h(K_\varepsilon)$ does not contain $u$ by [F8]. If it is nonempty, the continuous function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ on that compact image attains a positive minimum by [F8]; continuity follows from $\big||v-u|-|w-u|\big|\leq|v-w|$. Therefore the image is separated from $u$; if it is empty the conclusion is immediate. For every sufficiently small $\delta$, the closed shell $\overline B_\delta$ misses $K_\varepsilon$, so $d_\delta\geq d(u)-\varepsilon$. Together with $d_\delta\leq d(u)$, this proves $d_\delta\to d(u)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, in particular along the matching sequence $\delta_j$. Step 1.2 now gives the iterated shell limit $-d(u)=s(u)$.

Let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_u$ and put $C:=\Delta(\mathcal A)\setminus U$, which is closed and hence compact by step 1.1 and [F7]. If $C\cap H_u=\varnothing$, then $h(C)$ is compact by [F8] and does not contain $u$; if $C$ is nonempty, the continuous function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ attains a positive minimum there by [F8], using $\big||v-u|-|w-u|\big|\leq|v-w|$. Thus sufficiently small shells miss $C$; this is also immediate when $C=\varnothing$. Otherwise, $C\cap H_u$ is a nonempty closed subset of the compact simplex and is compact by [F7]. Continuity of $D$ and [F8] give $d_C:=\min_{C\cap H_u}D>d(u)$, since $C$ contains no constrained minimizer. Choose $0<\eta<d_C-d(u)$ and set $K:=\{q\in C:D(q\|p)\leq d(u)+\eta\}$; it is closed and hence compact by [F4] and [F7], and it is disjoint from $H_u$. Therefore $h(K)$ is compact by [F8] and does not contain $u$. If empty it is already separated from $u$; otherwise, the continuous distance function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ attains a positive minimum there by [F8], so $h(K)$ is separated from $u$. Hence for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $\inf_{C\cap\overline B_\delta}D\geq d(u)+\eta$. For every sufficiently small matching radius $\delta_j$, we also have $d_{\delta_j}<d(u)+\eta/2$. The LDP upper bound [F2] on the closed set $\overline{C\cap B_{\delta_j}}\subseteq C\cap\overline B_{\delta_j}$ bounds the numerator's logarithmic limsup exponent by $-d(u)-\eta$. By step 1.2 the denominator's logarithmic limit exponent is $-d_{\delta_j}$, so subtracting gives a conditional logarithmic limsup at most $d_{\delta_j}-d(u)-\eta<-\eta/2$. Thus for every sufficiently large $j$ the conditional probability tends to zero exponentially as $n\to\infty$, which gives the asserted iterated concentration limit.

Conversely, let $u$ maximize $s(v)-\beta v$ and let $q\in\mathcal M_u$. For any $r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, put $v=h(r)$. Then $D(r)+\beta v\geq d(v)+\beta v\geq d(u)+\beta u=D(q)+\beta u$, so $q\in\mathcal M_\beta$. This proves both the equality of energy sets and the macrostate criterion. Rearranging $s(v)-\beta v\leq s(u)-\beta u$ gives exactly $s(v)\leq s(u)+\beta(v-u)$; hence the criterion is the stated upper-supporting-line condition, with no formal inverse-transform assumption.
