Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

Use the finite exponential family, minimality, convex hull, affine hull, and relative-interior definitions from the A-page finite-family Definition. Assume the representation is minimal. The sample space is $X^n$ with product mass $\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_\theta(x_i)$, which is the IID sampling model; $n\ge1$. For a realized tuple $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$, set $\bar T=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nT(x_i)$ and $K=\operatorname{conv}(T(X))$. A finite MLE is a parameter $\hat\theta\in\mathbb R^k$ attaining the maximum of that likelihood. Then a finite MLE exists if and only if $\bar T\in\operatorname{ri}K$, and when it exists it is unique.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: The two statistic values are $-1$ and $+1$, so their affine hull is $\mathbb R$, the family is minimal, the convex hull is $[-1,1]$, and the sample mean is $1$, which is not in its interior $(-1,1)$. Hence [F2] already implies there is no finite MLE.

Let $S(h)=e^h+e^{-h}$. Both exponential terms and hence $S(h)$ are positive by [F7]. For the fixed all-plus IID sample the product likelihood is $L(h)=\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_h(+1)=(e^h/S(h))^n>0$ by [A1, F1]. Applying the positive-product law [F8] repeatedly to these $n\ge1$ factors, then its quotient law and the inverse identity [F7], gives $\log L(h)=n(\log(e^h)-\log S(h))=n(h-\log S(h))=\ell(h)$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing, this has exactly the same maximizers as $L$. By [F3] and [F5], the two exponential terms have derivatives $e^h$ and $-e^{-h}$; [F6] therefore gives $S'(h)=e^h-e^{-h}$. The identity function has derivative $1$ directly from its difference quotient. Applying the logarithm derivative [F4] and chain rule [F5] to this derived log likelihood gives
$\ell'(h)=n\left(1-\frac{e^h-e^{-h}}{e^h+e^{-h}}\right)
=\frac{2ne^{-h}}{e^h+e^{-h}}>0$
for every finite $h$. The derived formula is differentiable on all of $\mathbb R$, hence continuous there: its increment is its convergent difference quotient times the real increment. For any $h_1<h_2$, [F9] applied on $[h_1,h_2]$ gives $\ell(h_2)-\ell(h_1)=\ell'(c)(h_2-h_1)>0$ for some $c\in(h_1,h_2)$. Thus $\ell$ is strictly increasing; by [F8] the likelihood also increases. In particular each finite field has a larger likelihood at a greater field, and no finite field maximizes it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For every $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the free finite-volume FK laws on $\Lambda_n$ are stochastically increasing under restriction as $n$ grows, and the wired finite-volume FK laws are stochastically decreasing under restriction. The probabilities of every finite-coordinate atom therefore have unique nonnegative normalized consistent numerical limits. Under Countable Choice, each limiting family extends uniquely to a probability measure on the cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra of $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$. Thus the free and wired infinite-volume states exist under this measure-extension hypothesis.

Let $q\geq1$ be a finite real number. On the nearest-neighbor square lattice let $\Lambda_n=\{-n,\ldots,n\}^2$, let $E_n$ consist of edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_\infty=n\}$. For $p\in(0,1)$ and a partition $\xi$ of $B_n$, give $A\subseteq E_n$ probability proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)}$, where $k_\xi$ counts components after the partition classes are identified. Write $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ for the free partition when $b=0$ and the one-class wired partition when $b=1$.

For every event $C$ determined by finitely many edge coordinates, the numerical limits
$$\pi^b_{p,q}(C):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(C),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},$$
exist. They are consistent, nonnegative normalized finite-coordinate probability families, invariant under translations and quarter-turns. On increasing cylinder events they are increasing in $p$, with $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$. Every cylinder-probability limit of arbitrary boundary partitions lies between these two families on increasing cylinder events. There is an at most countable set $D_q\subset(0,1)$ such that $\pi^0_{p,q}(C)=\pi^1_{p,q}(C)$ for every cylinder event $C$ whenever $p\notin D_q$.

Let $D_r$ be the event that actual open edges inside $\Lambda_r$ join $0$ to $B_r$, and define the real numbers
$$\Theta_b(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^b_{p,q}(D_r).$$
Then $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$ for $0<p<p'<1$, and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^1_{n,p,q}(0\leftrightarrow B_n)=\Theta_1(p,q).$$
Connections here use actual edges, not artificial boundary-identification paths. These are statements about real limits and finite probability tables; existence of a countably additive probability on the infinite configuration space is not asserted.

Let $E_\infty$ be the nearest-neighbor edge set of $\mathbb Z^2$, and let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$. Let $E_n$ contain the edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $\partial\Lambda_n$ be the vertices of $\Lambda_n$ adjacent to a vertex outside it. Fix $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$. For each boundary partition $\xi_n$ on $\partial\Lambda_n$, let $\phi_{n,p,q}^{\xi_n}$ be the finite FK law on $(\Lambda_n,E_n)$ with mass proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_{\xi_n}(A)}$ for $A\subseteq E_n$, where $k_{\xi_n}(A)$ counts components after wiring the partition classes and extend its configurations to $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ by setting all edges outside $E_n$ closed.

An **infinite-volume FK state** at $(p,q)$ is any probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ that is a cylinder-probability limit of such extended finite-volume laws along a sequence $n_j\to\infty$ and boundary partitions $\xi_{n_j}$. Cylinder-probability convergence means convergence of the probability of every assignment on every finite set of edges. When they exist, the **free FK state** and **wired FK state** are the cylinder limits for the identity and one-class partitions, respectively, at every $n$. Their existence and uniqueness as probability-measure cylinder limits are established by a later A-page lemma under its stated measure-extension hypothesis. For either state $\phi^b_{p,q}$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, define $\theta^b(p,q):=\phi^b_{p,q}(0\leftrightarrow\infty)$, where $0\leftrightarrow\infty$ means that the open cluster of the origin is not contained in any finite box, and define

$$p_c^b(q):=\inf\{p\in(0,1):\theta^b(p,q)>0\}.$$

No equality of free and wired states at $p=p_c$ is part of this definition.

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

Let $q\geq1$ be real, $p\in(0,1)$, $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, and $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ the finite square-lattice FK law with free boundary partition $b=0$ or wired partition $b=1$. All paths below use actual open lattice edges, not artificial wiring edges. For each cylinder event $A$ let $\pi^b_{p,q}(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(A)$ be its numerical cylinder limit. Put $p_s=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $D_r$ be the cylinder event that $0$ connects inside $\Lambda_r$ to its vertex boundary. Then $a_n(p,q)=\phi^1_{n,p,q}(D_n)$ decreases, and
$$\Theta^1(p,q):=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r).$$
For $p>p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)>0$; for $p<p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)=0$. Consequently $\inf\{p\in(0,1):\Theta^1(p,q)>0\}=p_s$. No value at $p_s$ is asserted. These numerical conclusions do not require Countable Choice or the extension of cylinder weights to an infinite-volume measure.

More precisely, fix $p>p_s$ and any real $\alpha>1$. Put $r_k=\lfloor\alpha^k\rfloor$. For all sufficiently large $k$, let $A_k$ be the cylinder event that an actual open simple circuit surrounds $\Lambda_{r_k}$, lies outside $\Lambda_{r_k}$ and strictly inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$, and is connected inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$ to its vertex boundary. There are $C,\varepsilon>0$ and an integer $K$ such that $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}<1/2$ for $k\geq K$ and, for every $n\geq m\geq N\geq K$,
$$\phi^1_{r_{n+2},p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq\prod_{k=N}^{n}(1-d_k),\qquad \pi^1_{p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq1-\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}d_k.$$
For $0<p<t<1$ and $H_n$ the finite Hamming distance to $D_n$, the finite cylinder expectation satisfies
$$\pi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{t,q}}H_n\}.$$
For every $0<s<p_s$ and every $d>0$, there are $C_d,n_d$ such that $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq C_d n^{-(2d+4)}$ for $n\geq n_d$. The expectation here is a finite sum of cylinder atom weights.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a given probability space. For each $y\in\mathbb Z^2$, let $S_y$ be a measurable random finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $y$, with the discrete sigma-algebra on the countable collection of such sets. Assume the sets $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed and that $\mathbb E|S_0|^r<\infty$ for every real $r>0$. A lattice animal is a finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $0$. Define the extended measurable envelope
$$M_z=\sup\{|S_y|:y\in\mathbb Z^2,\ z\in S_y\}.$$
Almost surely every $M_z$ is a finite maximum, and there is a deterministic finite constant $K_0$ such that, almost surely, every sufficiently large lattice animal $\Gamma$ satisfies
$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|.$$
More generally, for any given independent identically distributed field $X_y\geq1$ with finite moments of every positive order, there is a deterministic finite $K$ such that almost surely $\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq K|\Gamma|$ for every sufficiently large lattice animal. The random cutoff may depend on the realization. This result assumes the stated random family on a probability space; it does not construct an infinite product law or require a choice axiom to supply that law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $A$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$. Fix a bijection $(i_n)_{n\geq1}:\mathbb N_{>0}	o\mathbb Z^d$ and give $X$ the metric
$$d_X(\sigma,\eta)=\sum_{n\geq1}2^{-n}\mathbf 1_{\{\sigma_{i_n}
e\eta_{i_n}\}}.$$
For a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and $B\subseteq A^F$, write $[F,B]=\{\sigma\in X:\sigma|_F\in B\}$ and let $\mathcal C=\{[F,B]:F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite},\ B\subseteq A^F\}$ be the cylinder algebra. A family $(
u_F)_{F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite}}$ of probability measures on $A^F$ is **consistent** if $(\pi_E^F)_*
u_F=
u_E$ whenever $E\subseteq F$, where $\pi_E^F:A^F	o A^E$ is restriction. Such a family defines $\mu_0([F,B])=
u_F(B)$; consistency makes this a well-defined normalized finitely additive probability on $\mathcal C$. Then $X$ is compact, the Borel sigma-algebra is $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, and $\mu_0$ extends uniquely to a probability on $\sigma(\mathcal C)$. Moreover, every sequence of probabilities on this sigma-algebra has a subsequence whose cylinder probabilities converge to those of a probability measure; along that subsequence integrals of every continuous $f:X	o\mathbb R$ converge.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

derivations.claim: Fix any $0<s<p_s:=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $R_x=\sup\{\lVert z-x\rVert_\infty:z\in C_x\}$, allowing infinity initially. The event $R_x\geq n$ is the translate of $D_n$: a path reaching that distance has an initial segment inside the centered box to its boundary. Its probability under the wired law is its numerical cylinder weight by [F1]. Thus [F3], with arbitrarily large $d$, gives polynomial tails of arbitrarily high order for $R_x$. Since $|C_x|\leq(2R_x+1)^2$, nonnegative monotone convergence applied to successive integer layers proves $\mathbb E_s^1|C_x|^d<\infty$ for every $d>0$; explicitly the layer bound for $R_x^{2d}$ is a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}n^{2d-1}P(R_x\geq n)$, which converges after choosing [F3] with that $d$. Every $C_x$ is finite almost surely, simultaneously at all countably many vertices. Translation invariance follows from the numerical cylinder identities in [F1] and uniqueness in [F5].

We establish a conditional cluster comparison before constructing a new law. Enumerate the vertices deterministically. Suppose a finite number of complete finite clusters have been discovered, with union $E$. Revealing their vertex sets says that each discovered set is connected by its internal open edges and every edge from it to its complement is closed. These are finite-edge events. In each finite FK box, after all edges between $E$ and its complement are fixed closed, the component factors and edge weights internal to $E$ factor from the remaining weights; summing over allowed internal configurations preserves that factorization. Hence the law outside $E$ depends on the discovered sets only through the closed boundary edges. Passing fixed finite-cylinder conditional probabilities to the wired limit proves the same identity there. A positive-probability history has a positive denominator because its defining finite edge event does; null histories may be assigned arbitrary normalized kernels and are never reached.

If the next vertex $y$ is outside $E$, its conditional cluster law is dominated, by inclusion of vertex sets, by the unconditional wired cluster law of $y$. Indeed in a finite box compare the original wired law with the same law constrained to close every edge from $E$ to its complement. The common-uniform heat-bath update in [F2] preserves order; fixed-closed coordinates stay below the upper chain, and all other conditional edge probabilities remain ordered. Taking stationary limits gives an ordered finite-box coupling. Apply [F5] to the pair of binary edge fields along growing boxes and take a joint cylinder limit. Its upper marginal is the wired law; its lower marginal outside $E$ is the conditional law in step 2.1, since conditioning a fixed positive-probability cylinder commutes with these limits. The order event is a countable intersection of coordinatewise closed conditions and holds in the limit. Project to the two clusters of $y$. Both are finite almost surely, by the upper marginal and step 1.1. This proves existence of an ordered coupling on pairs of finite connected vertex sets for each possible positive-probability history.

The possible finite histories, finite connected lattice sets, and pairs of such sets have explicit countable encodings by integer vertex lists. Apply [A1] to the fixed countable family of nonempty sets of coupling kernels from step 3.1, choosing one kernel for every history in advance. At a stage whose vertex $y$ is already discovered, its actual-cluster output is its earlier cluster and the second output is a fresh independent set with the unconditional cluster law of $y$. At an undiscovered $y$, use its selected ordered kernel: its first marginal is the conditional cluster law from step 2.1 and its second marginal is again that fixed unconditional law. Each kernel is a probability on a countable set of pairs of finite sets. The product of the successive kernels defines normalized consistent finite-prefix atomic probabilities; summing the last kernel's mass one verifies consistency. A kernel's second marginal is fixed for every history, including the earlier second outputs, so these second outputs have product marginals for every finite list of stages. Countable Choice here selects kernels for a countable set fixed in advance, rather than successive unspecified choices from a relation.

Here is an explicit extension of the process, to avoid assuming a countable-alphabet extension theorem. Enumerate each stage's possible output pairs by integers $j\geq0$, and encode $j$ by a bit row consisting of $j$ ones, a zero, and then zeros. For every finite set of coordinates in the countable array of bits, sum the appropriate finite-prefix atomic probabilities from step 4.1. All sums are nonnegative countable sums over explicitly enumerated finite tuples of integers. Summing the last kernel verifies consistency of the binary finite-dimensional laws. Identify the bit array with the countable coordinates in [F5] and extend under [A1]. For a given row the weight of its first $K$ bits being all ones is the atomic tail $P(j\geq K)$, tending to zero, so the all-ones row has probability zero by countable additivity. Each finite pattern having a one after its first zero also has prescribed probability zero. A countable union shows that almost surely every row is a valid integer code. Decode on this measurable full-probability set, assigning a fixed default on its null complement. The resulting process has exactly the specified finite-prefix laws. This constructs the required law without an additional invocation of a process-extension or independent-uniform theorem.

Write $S_y$ for the second output at the stage of $y$, and $\widehat C_z$ for the actual cluster assigned by the first outputs. Step 4.1 shows that the $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed as the translated wired cluster; their sizes have all moments by step 1.1. The first outputs have precisely the original wired cluster-exploration laws by induction on every finite prefix. The complete cluster at each fixed $z$ is assigned by the stage reaching $z$, so all finite lists of complete cluster sets have the actual wired joint law. Equality of the whole countably indexed cluster-set law follows as well: unary encode these finite-set labels; its binary cylinder values determine its law uniquely by [F5]. Whenever a new cluster is discovered at $y$, it is a subset of $S_y$ by the ordered kernel. Every $z$ in that cluster therefore satisfies $|\widehat C_z|\leq M_z:=\sup\{|S_y|:z\in S_y\}$. The enumeration eventually assigns every vertex. This coupled object is a cluster partition, not an edge configuration reconstructed from clusters.

Apply [F4] to the given independent family $S_y$ on the constructed probability space. There is a deterministic finite $K_0$ such that almost surely all sufficiently large animals $\Gamma$ satisfy $\sum_{z\in\Gamma}|\widehat C_z|\leq\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|$. This countably measurable property of the cluster partition transfers to the actual wired law by step 6.1. An animal is a finite connected vertex set containing $0$, so this applies simultaneously to every sufficiently long self-avoiding path starting at $0$. No claim that the dependent envelope variables are independent is made.

In any edge configuration with such a cluster partition, let $\gamma$ be a self-avoiding path from $0$ to $\partial\Lambda_n$, with $m$ vertices. It has $m\geq n+1$. If it visits $J$ distinct open clusters, its number $T(\gamma)$ of closed edges is at least $J-1$. Each visited cluster $C$ contributes at most one to $\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}$, because the path visits distinct vertices. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives $T(\gamma)+1\geq\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}\geq m^2/(\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|)\geq m/K_0$ for all sufficiently long paths, by step 7.1. The subtraction of one is necessary even for a path contained in a single cluster. Since this inequality holds for every edge configuration with that partition, transferring the partition law was sufficient; no internal open edges had to be selected in the coupling.

A path minimizing the number of closed edges in the finite box may be taken self-avoiding by erasing loops without increasing that number. The uniform large-animal cutoff in step 7.1 and step 8.1 give $H_n\geq(n+1)/K_0-1$ for all sufficiently large $n$, almost surely in the actual wired law at $s$. Fatou's inequality from [F6], applied to the nonnegative measurable variables $H_n/n$, gives $\liminf_n\mathbb E_s^1H_n/n\geq1/K_0$. Thus for all sufficiently large deterministic $n$, $\mathbb E_s^1H_n\geq n/(2K_0)$. This expectation conclusion does not assume a deterministic bound on the random almost-sure cutoff.

Now fix the parameter $p$ in the statement and choose $s\in(p,p_s)$. The preceding moment, coupling, and Hamming-expectation arguments apply at this $s$. Since $H_n$ is a finite-coordinate function, its expectation under the wired Borel law is exactly the finite sum of its numerical cylinder atom weights in [F3]. That supplier's Hamming inequality therefore gives $\phi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-2(s-p)n/K_0\}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Increasing a prefactor covers all $n\geq1$. In particular the probability of an infinite cluster at $0$ is zero: that event is contained in every $D_n$, whose probabilities tend to zero.

By translation invariance, the same one-arm bound holds at every center. If $x\ne y$ and $r=\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty$, any finite open path from $x$ to $y$ has an initial segment from $x$ to the vertex boundary of $x+\Lambda_r$ inside that box. Thus its wired connection probability is at most the translated one-arm bound at radius $r$. Since $r\geq\lVert x-y\rVert_2/\sqrt2$, changing constants proves $\phi^1_{p,q}(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}$, also for $x=y$ after enlarging $C$.

Let $\phi$ be any cylinder limit in the statement. An increasing event supported on a fixed inner box has finite-volume conditional laws with boundary partitions at most wired; passing its cylinder probabilities to the limit bounds them above by the wired inner-box law. Then increase that inner box to infinity, using the wired cylinder limit in [F1], to obtain domination by the wired state on increasing cylinder events. The event that $x$ connects $y$ by a path in a fixed box is such an event. These events increase to $\{x\leftrightarrow y\}$ as boxes grow; countable additivity, or [F6] applied to their indicators, therefore gives the identical upper bound in step 11.1 for $\phi$. Similarly the translated $D_n$ events dominate any infinite cluster at their center, giving probability zero. Constants depend only on $p,q$, not on the cylinder-limit state. The proof has made no assertion at $p_s$ and has used Countable Choice exactly in the stated extensions and kernel selection.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Write $z=t+is$ with $0\leq s\leq1$. The spectral multiplier $f_z(\lambda)=\exp(-iz\log(\lambda)/2)$ has $|f_z(\lambda)|^2=\lambda^s$. Since $\lambda^s\leq1+\lambda$ for every $\lambda>0$ and $s\in[0,1]$, [F2] gives $$\|A^{-iz/2}\xi\|^2=\int\lambda^s\,d\mu_\xi\leq\int(1+\lambda)\,d\mu_\xi=\|\xi\|^2+\|A^{1/2}\xi\|^2.$$ This also proves that every vector named in the Statement is in the domain of the indicated multiplier.

If $z_n=t_n+is_n\to z=t+is$ in $S$, then $f_{z_n}(\lambda)\to f_z(\lambda)$ pointwise and $$|f_{z_n}(\lambda)-f_z(\lambda)|^2\leq2\lambda^{s_n}+2\lambda^s\leq4(1+\lambda).$$ The majorant is integrable by $\xi\in D(A^{1/2})$. Dominated convergence applied to the scalar spectral measure therefore gives $\|A^{-iz_n/2}\xi-A^{-iz/2}\xi\|^2\to0$, proving strong continuity on the closed strip.

Fix $z_0$ with $s_0=\operatorname{Im}z_0\in(0,1)$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $2\delta<s_0<1-2\delta$. For $|h|\leq\delta$, the scalar difference quotient of $f_z(\lambda)$ along the segment from $z_0$ to $z_0+h$ is bounded by $$\frac12|\log\lambda|\sup_{0\leq r\leq1}\lambda^{\operatorname{Im}(z_0+rh)/2}.$$ When $0<\lambda\leq1$ this is bounded by $\frac12|\log\lambda|\lambda^{\delta/2}$, and when $\lambda\geq1$ it is bounded by $\frac12|\log\lambda|\lambda^{(1-\delta)/2}$. The first expression has a finite supremum and the second is bounded by a constant depending on $\delta$ times $\lambda^{1/2}$. Thus the difference quotients are dominated in $L^2(\mu_\xi)$ by a constant times $1+\lambda^{1/2}$. Their pointwise limit is $(-i/2)(\log\lambda)f_{z_0}(\lambda)$. Dominated convergence in the spectral norm proves that the vector difference quotient converges in $H$ to the spectral integral of this limit. Hence the vector map is complex-differentiable at $z_0$.
Step 2.2 applies at every point of $S^\circ$, so the vector map is norm-holomorphic throughout the open strip. The estimate and closed-strip continuity were proved in steps 1.1 and 2.1.

For xi=0 the scalar spectral measure is zero, so the norm integral in1.1 and difference integrals in2.1–2.2 vanish and the vector function is identically zero. A zero A on a nonzero space is excluded by spectral support on the positive half-line.
For A=I, the spectral measure is concentrated at lambda=1 and every multiplier in1.1 equals one; the orbit is constant xi and its norm-holomorphic derivative is zero. This includes one-dimensional H.

No simple spectrum is needed:1.1 and2.1 integrate scalar measures and2.2 uses only positive spectral values and the square-root moment. Repeated eigenvalues and continuous spectral multiplicity leave these bounds unchanged.
Closed-strip continuity is proved at Im z=0 and Im z=1; holomorphy is restricted to the open strip (step 2.1).

Choice is declared in the Statement and A1 and enters through F1 spectral resolution and F2 unbounded Borel calculus in1.1; the subsequent scalar dominated-convergence steps do not assert an extra family selection.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero vector, reshape its coefficient array as a matrix with row index $i_1$ and column index $(i_2,\ldots,i_N)$. By [F1] this gives an exact finite sum of products of a first-site coefficient and a residual coefficient array. Reshape the residual array at site $2$ with row index $(a_1,i_2)$ and remaining sites as column index, apply [F1] again, and store the resulting left coefficient array as the entries of $A_2^{i_2}$ with virtual indices $(a_1,a_2)$. Repeating this finite operation through site $N-1$ leaves a final array defining $A_N^{i_N}$; every SVD factorization is exact, so the original coefficient of each ordered product-basis vector is the displayed matrix product. For $N=1$ take the coefficients as scalar matrices. For the zero vector take all bond dimensions equal to $1$ and set the first site matrices to zero. Thus all finite vectors admit the stated representation.

For any integer $q\ge1$ and positive semidefinite $Y\in M_q(\mathbb C)\otimes M_D(\mathbb C)$, the amplification is $({\rm id}_{M_q}\otimes\mathcal E)(Y)=\sum_{i=1}^d(I_q\otimes A^i)Y(I_q\otimes A^{i*})$. Each summand is positive semidefinite, so every amplification is positive and $\mathcal E$ is completely positive. The displayed definition also fixes its exact input and output spaces and makes no trace-preserving or unitality assertion.

The map $\Gamma_L$ is linear and its image is a finite-dimensional subspace of $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes L}$. By [F2], choose an orthonormal basis $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ of that image and define $P_Lv:=\sum_{a=1}^s\langle v,u_a\rangle u_a$. Orthonormality gives $P_L^*=P_L$ and $P_L^2=P_L$, and $v-P_Lv$ is orthogonal to every $u_a$. Thus $h_L=I-P_L$ is the orthogonal projection onto the complement, with $\langle h_Lv,v\rangle=\|h_Lv\|^2\ge0$ and kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$.

Fix a finite open MPS made from the same tensor and a block of $L$ consecutive sites. For each fixed physical-basis configuration outside that block, contraction of the outside tensors leaves a row $\alpha$ on the left and a column $\beta$ on the right. With $X=\beta\alpha$, direct coordinates give $\operatorname{tr}(XA^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})=\sum_{u,v}\beta_u\alpha_v(A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})_{vu}=\alpha A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L}\beta$, so that block slice is $\Gamma_L(X)$. The outside basis configurations are orthonormal, so the full vector is a sum of outside basis vectors tensored with block vectors in $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$; the corresponding $h_L$ therefore annihilates it. Each term in $H_{N,L}$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.3, and their sum annihilates the MPS. If that vector is nonzero, zero is an eigenvalue and the minimum possible energy, so the vector is a zero-energy ground state. The zero vector is annihilated but supplies no eigenstate: for example, if all tensor matrices vanish, then $\Gamma_L=0$, $h_L=I$ and $H_{N,L}=(N-L+1)I$, whose ground energy is positive. No uniqueness or positive-gap conclusion for a nonzero MPS follows from this argument.

Let $Q\in\{2,3,4\}$ and let $L\geq1$ be an integer. The finite Potts-clock space is
$$\mathcal H_{Q,L}:=(\mathbb C^Q)^{\otimes L}$$
of dimension $Q^L$, with the tensor-product Hermitian inner product taken linear in its first argument and computational orthonormal basis
$$|a_1,\ldots,a_L\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_L\rangle,\qquad a_j\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}.$$
On $\mathbb C^Q$, this inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}x_a\overline{y_a}$, and on elementary tensors it is $\langle u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_L,v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_L\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^L\langle u_j,v_j\rangle$.
For a unit vector $u$, the notation $|u\rangle\langle u|$ denotes the endomorphism $v\mapsto\langle v,u\rangle u$. On one site use the clock and shift convention
$$R_Q|a\rangle=e^{2\pi i a/Q}|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$

$$D_{j,j+1}:=\sum_{a=0}^{Q-1}|aa\rangle\langle aa|$$
act on factors $j,j+1$ and as identity on the others. The open-chain local operators are
$$e_{2j-1}:=\sqrt Q\,P_j\quad(1\leq j\leq L),\qquad e_{2j}:=\sqrt Q\,D_{j,j+1}\quad(1\leq j<L).$$

For real coefficients $J_1,\ldots,J_{2L-1}$, define the weighted open-chain matrix
$$H_{Q,L}(\mathbf J):=-\sum_{i=1}^{2L-1}J_i e_i.$$
It is an endomorphism of $\mathcal H_{Q,L}$. For an endomorphism $T$ of this inner-product space, $T^*$ is its adjoint, characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$; $T$ is self-adjoint (Hermitian) exactly when $T=T^*$. An endomorphism is normal exactly when $TT^*=T^*T$, so every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal. For a subspace $W\subseteq\mathcal H_{Q,L}$, the orthogonal projection onto $W$ sends $w+z$ to $w$ in the unique decomposition $\mathcal H_{Q,L}=W\oplus W^\perp$, with $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$. Viewed as an endomorphism, it satisfies $\Pi_W^2=\Pi_W=\Pi_W^*$; the adjoint identity follows from the orthogonality of the two summands. A self-adjoint endomorphism $A$ is positive definite if $\langle Av,v\rangle>0$ for every nonzero $v$, and is positive semidefinite exactly when $\langle Av,v\rangle\geq0$ for every $v$; these quadratic forms are real because $A=A^*$. The trace $\operatorname{tr}(T)$ of a finite-dimensional endomorphism is the basis-independent sum of diagonal entries of its matrix.

Every $\lambda\in\Lambda(H_{Q,L})$ is real: for a unit eigenvector $v$, $\lambda=\langle H_{Q,L}v,v\rangle=\langle v,H_{Q,L}v\rangle=\overline\lambda$. $$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], every defining relation of $P_{2L}(\mathbb C,\delta)$ is satisfied by the operators $e_i$; the quotient presentation in [F3] therefore gives the stated Temperley-Lieb representation.

For each $i$, $g_i-qI=-e_i$ and $g_i+q^{-1}I=\delta I-e_i$. Hence $$(g_i-qI)(g_i+q^{-1}I)=-e_i(\delta I-e_i)=e_i^2-\delta e_i=0$$ by [F2] and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. This is the Hecke quadratic relation in [F4]'s normalization.

For adjacent $i,i+1$, expand with $e=e_i$ and $f=e_{i+1}$. Using $e^2=\delta e$, $f^2=\delta f$, $efe=e$, and $fef=f$ from [F2], direct multiplication gives $$g_ig_{i+1}g_i-g_{i+1}g_ig_{i+1}=(-q^2+q\delta-1)(e_i-e_{i+1}).$$ Since [A1] gives $q\delta=q(q+q^{-1})=q^2+1$, this difference is zero.
If $|i-j|>1$, [F2] gives $e_ie_j=e_je_i$, so their affine combinations $g_i=qI-e_i$ and $g_j=qI-e_j$ commute.

When $Q=4$, [F1] selects $q=1$ and $\delta=2$. Then $g_i=I-e_i$ and $$g_i^2=(I-e_i)^2=I-2e_i+e_i^2=I$$ by [F2]. Steps 1.3–1.4 give the adjacent braid and distant-commutation relations. Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\rho_{ABC}$ be a density operator on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$. With $S$ and $I(A:C\mid B)$ as defined in [[def-qsmx-information-conventions]],

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC})\ge0.$$

Also let $d,e\ge1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be a finite completely positive trace-preserving map. For all positive semidefinite $X,Y\in M_d(\mathbb C)$,

$$D(\Phi(X)\|\Phi(Y))\le D(X\|Y),$$

where $D$ is the support-sensitive finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy: it equals $\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$ when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, and $+\infty$ otherwise. These are finite-dimensional mathematical statements. The channel inequality is one-sided and asserts no equality condition, recovery map, or infinite-dimensional extension.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: The linear map $\mathcal L$ acts on a finite-dimensional normed space, so its exponential series converges absolutely in operator norm, uniformly on bounded time intervals. For $u,v\geq0$, the Cauchy product and binomial theorem give $T_uT_v=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{m+n=k}\frac{u^m v^n}{m!n!}\right)\mathcal L^k=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(u+v)^k}{k!}\mathcal L^k=T_{u+v}$. Now let $0\leq s\leq t$ and put $u=t-s$, $v=s$. The map $T_{t-s}$ is a finite channel by the hypothesis and [F1], and it fixes $\sigma$ by stationarity. Apply [A1] to $X=T_s\rho$ and $Y=\sigma$; these are positive semidefinite, and therefore $D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)\leq D(T_s\rho\|\sigma)$. This proves global monotonicity, including singular initial densities, because $\sigma>0$ makes every displayed relative entropy finite.

For $x>0$ and $R>0$, direct integration gives $\int_0^R((1+s)^{-1}-(x+s)^{-1})\,ds=\log x+\log(1+R)-\log(x+R)$, which tends to $\log x$ as $R\to\infty$. Applying this scalar identity to each eigenvalue using [F2] yields $\log A=\int_0^\infty((1+s)^{-1}I-(A+sI)^{-1})\,ds$ for positive definite $A$. Write $X=\dot A(u)$. Differentiating $(A+sI)(A+sI)^{-1}=I$ gives $\frac{d}{du}(A+sI)^{-1}=-(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1}$, so $\frac{d}{du}\log A=\int_0^\infty(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1}\,ds$. Differentiation under this integral is justified locally when the least eigenvalue of $A$ is bounded below by $m>0$, because the integrand norm is at most $\|X\|(m+s)^{-2}$ and this bound is integrable. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{du}\operatorname{Tr}(A\log A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log A)+\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Tr}(A(A+sI)^{-1}X(A+sI)^{-1})\,ds$. Diagonalize $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j>0$; the integral is $\sum_j X_{jj}\int_0^\infty\lambda_j(\lambda_j+s)^{-2}\,ds=\sum_jX_{jj}=\operatorname{Tr}X$. Hence $\frac{d}{du}\operatorname{Tr}(A\log A)=\operatorname{Tr}(X(\log A+I))$.

For $f(t):=D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)$, every quotient $(f(t+h)-f(t))/h$ with $h>0$ is nonpositive by step 1.1. Thus $D^+f(t):=\limsup_{h\downarrow0}(f(t+h)-f(t))/h\leq0$ as an extended-real upper right Dini derivative, without inserting $\log\rho_t$ when $\rho_t$ is singular.

Its sign is nonpositive because the same function is nonincreasing by step 1.1.

$$G'(t_0)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A'(t_0)(\log A(t_0)+I_H)\right),$$

where $I_H$ is the identity endomorphism of $H$ and $A'(t_0)$ is obtained by differentiating the matrix entries in the fixed basis.

Define the modular-energy difference relative to $\sigma$ by $\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma):=\operatorname{tr}((\rho-\sigma)K_\sigma)$. Then

$$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma)-(s(\rho)-s(\sigma)).$$

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\rho\|\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\sigma)\le D(\rho\|\sigma).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Since $\rho$ is entrywise continuous at $0$, its finite matrix difference $T(\varepsilon):=\rho(\varepsilon)-\sigma$ tends to zero in operator norm: in a fixed orthonormal basis, if every entry of $T$ has magnitude at most $M$, then for a unit vector $x$ $\sum_j|x_j|^2=1$ makes each coordinate of $x$ have magnitude at most $1$, and each coordinate of $Tx$ has magnitude at most $dM$, and therefore $\|Tx\|\le d^{3/2}M$, where $d=\dim H$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $\|T(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}<m/2$ for $|\varepsilon|<\delta$. For each $v\in H$, $\langle\sigma v,v\rangle\ge m\|v\|^2$ by spectral decomposition, while [F5] and [F6] give $|\langle T(\varepsilon)v,v\rangle|\le\|T(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|^2$. Hence $\langle\rho(\varepsilon)v,v\rangle>(m/2)\|v\|^2$ for nonzero $v$. Thus $\rho(\varepsilon)$ is positive definite near $0$ and [F1] applies.

Apply [F1] to $\rho$ at $0$: $\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}s(\rho(\varepsilon))\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0)(\log\sigma+I))$. Because $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\varepsilon))=1$ on the whole interval, in the fixed basis [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0))=\sum_i\rho'_{ii}(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\sum_i(\rho_{ii}(h)-\rho_{ii}(0))/h=\lim_{h\to0}(1-1)/h=0$; the finite sum commutes with this limit. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with a fixed orthonormal basis, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, and let $t_0\in J$. Suppose $A:J\to\operatorname{End}(H)$ has real and imaginary matrix entries in the fixed basis differentiable at $t_0$ and is self-adjoint with strictly positive eigenvalues on a neighborhood of $t_0$. Define $\log A(t)$ by applying the natural logarithm to the eigenvalues of $A(t)$ in its spectral decomposition, let $\operatorname{tr}$ be the finite-dimensional trace, and let $\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|$ be the operator norm. Then $G(t):=\operatorname{tr}(A(t)\log A(t))$ is differentiable at $t_0$ and

$$G'(t_0)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A'(t_0)(\log A(t_0)+I_H)\right),$$

where $I_H$ is the identity endomorphism of $H$ and $A'(t_0)$ is obtained by differentiating the matrix entries in the fixed basis.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[lem-tgrx-finite-matrix-entropy-variation]]: for a differentiable path of self-adjoint positive-definite matrices, $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(\log\rho+I))$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Let $\rho,\sigma:H\to H$ be self-adjoint linear maps with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one, and suppose every eigenvalue of $\sigma$ is strictly positive. Define $K_\sigma:=-\log\sigma$ by spectral calculus, and for any self-adjoint $\tau:H\to H$ with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one define $s(\tau):=-\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\tau)=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with the zero-eigenvalue term $0\log0:=0$ and natural logarithms, so the entropy is in nats. Define the modular-energy difference relative to $\sigma$ by $\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma):=\operatorname{tr}((\rho-\sigma)K_\sigma)$. Then

$$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma)-(s(\rho)-s(\sigma)).$$

For any nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ with $H=H_A\otimes H_B$, partial tracing both states over $H_B$ cannot increase relative entropy:

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\rho\|\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\sigma)\le D(\rho\|\sigma).$$

The identity and inequality are finite-dimensional mathematical statements; no Hamiltonian, physical energy, physical units, continuum limit, or gravitational entropy is assumed.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[prop-tgrx-finite-modular-balance]]: for each density endomorphism $\tau$ and the fixed faithful reference $\sigma$, $D(\tau\|\sigma)=\operatorname{tr}((\tau-\sigma)K_\sigma)-(s(\tau)-s(\sigma))$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]: finite-dimensional Hermitian endomorphisms have orthonormal spectral decompositions, and the eigenvalues of a strictly positive one have a positive minimum.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]: trace is the finite sum of diagonal entries and therefore is linear.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[def-operator-norm]]: $\|Tv\|\le\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|$ for every vector $v$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.
